# Arne Furumark: Architect of Aegean Chronology
## Introduction
In the discipline of Aegean prehistory, few names command the foundational authority of Arne Furumark. A Swedish archaeologist and classical scholar, Furumark is universally recognized for establishing the typological and chronological framework that continues to govern the study of Mycenaean pottery and, by extension, the dating of the Late Bronze Age in the Eastern Mediterranean . His career, spanning the middle decades of the 20th century, bridged the gap between the pioneering, often romanticized excavations of the early 1900s and the rigorous, data-driven methodologies of modern archaeology. Through his monumental publications, particularly *The Mycenaean Pottery: Analysis and Classification* (1941) and *The Chronology of Mycenaean Pottery* (1941), Furumark provided the "grammar" and "syntax" for Late Helladic ceramics, creating a standardized system of "Furumark Shapes" (FS) and "Furumark Motifs" (FM) that remains the international standard .

Furumark’s influence extends beyond the library and the catalog. As a field archaeologist, he directed excavations at Sinda in Cyprus and San Giovenale in Italy, applying his chronological systems to complex stratigraphic realities . His work at Sinda offered crucial insights into the tumultuous end of the Bronze Age and the phenomenon of the "Sea Peoples," while his investigations in Italy helped synchronize the indigenous Italic chronologies with the Aegean sequence, fundamentally altering the understanding of the "Protovillanovan" period . Furthermore, Furumark was an active participant in the decipherment and interpretation of Linear B, engaging directly with the philological breakthroughs of the 1950s .

Despite the enduring utility of his systems, Furumark’s legacy is not without complexity. His approach, characterized by a meticulous, almost mathematical analysis of stylistic evolution, has been critiqued by later scholars for its rigidity and "dirigiste" nature . Yet, even these critiques acknowledge that any modification or refinement of Mycenaean chronology must inevitably begin with Furumark’s work. This report provides an exhaustive examination of Arne Furumark’s life, his methodological innovations, his archaeological fieldwork, and the lasting impact of his scholarship on the understanding of the ancient Mediterranean.

## Biography and Academic Trajectory
### Early Life and Formative Years
Born Josef Arne Gerdt Furumark on September 26, 1903, in Kristiania (modern Oslo), Norway, Furumark was the son of a Swedish father engaged in the paper industry . His early years were marked by a tension between familial expectations and personal intellectual ambition. While his family initially steered him toward a career in the paper business, Furumark’s interests were firmly rooted in the humanities . This early conflict perhaps instilled in him the disciplined work ethic that would later define his massive data-processing capabilities in adulthood.

In 1925, Furumark matriculated at Uppsala University in Sweden, an institution that would become his academic home for the remainder of his life . The intellectual climate at Uppsala during the interwar period was vibrant, particularly in the field of classical archaeology. Sweden was in the midst of a "golden age" of archaeological exploration, having established itself as a leading nation in prehistoric research through major excavations in Greece and Cyprus .

### The Influence of Axel W. Persson
At Uppsala, Furumark studied under the tutelage of Axel W. Persson, a towering figure in Swedish archaeology . Persson was renowned for his excavations at Asine and Dendra in the Argolid, sites that yielded spectacular finds, including unplundered tholos tombs and rich settlement deposits. Persson’s work provided the raw material and the inspiration for Furumark’s future research. Unlike the site-specific reports typical of the era, Furumark was encouraged to think synthetically, looking for patterns that transcended individual excavations.

Persson’s mentorship was instrumental in directing Furumark toward the study of Aegean decorative art. The massive quantities of pottery recovered from Asine needed systematic organization, and the existing frameworks—derived largely from Arthur Evans’s work on Crete—were increasingly inadequate for the mainland material. Furumark’s doctoral research began as an attempt to understand the stylistic antecedents of Mycenaean decoration, a project that would culminate in his 1939 dissertation, *Studies in Aegean Decorative Art: Antecedents and Sources of the Mycenaean Ceramic Decoration*.1 This thesis was not merely a student project but a prelude to his magnum opus, establishing the theoretical basis for his analysis of pictorial versus abstract art in the Aegean.

### The War Years and the "Magnum Opus"
Following the completion of his doctorate in 1939, Furumark was appointed as an associate professor (docent) at Uppsala University . The outbreak of World War II isolated Sweden from the Mediterranean, halting fieldwork and complicating international scholarly communication. However, this period of enforced confinement proved intellectually fertile for Furumark. With access to the library resources at Uppsala and the accumulated data from Swedish excavations, he dedicated the war years to the synthesis of Mycenaean pottery.

In 1941, amidst the conflict engulfing Europe, Furumark published the two volumes that would define his career: *The Mycenaean Pottery: Analysis and Classification* and *The Chronology of Mycenaean Pottery*.1 The publication of these works was a watershed moment. As noted by a contemporary reviewer in the *American Journal of Archaeology*, Furumark’s work was received with "awe" as a book that seemingly "solved all the problems of Mycenaean pottery" . The sheer ambition of the project—to catalog, classify, and date the entire corpus of known Mycenaean ceramics—established Furumark as the preeminent authority on the subject.

### Professorship and Institutional Leadership
Furumark’s academic ascent continued in the post-war era. In 1952, he was appointed Professor of Classical Archaeology and Ancient History at Uppsala University, succeeding his mentor’s generation . He held this chair until his retirement in 1970 . As a professor, Furumark cultivated the "Uppsala School" of archaeology, mentoring notable scholars such as Paul Åström and Sture Brunnsåker .

His leadership extended beyond the university. He served as the Director of the Swedish Institute at Athens from 1956 to 1957, reinforcing the strong archaeological ties between Sweden and Greece . In 1958, his contributions to science were formally recognized with his election as a member of the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences . Throughout the 1950s and 1960s, Furumark maintained an active correspondence with the international scholarly community, including key figures in the decipherment of Linear B like Michael Ventris and John Chadwick .

### Later Years and Posthumous Legacy
The later phase of Furumark’s career was marred by health issues. A period of serious illness in the late 1960s reduced his capacity for work and eventually led to his retirement in 1970 . Consequently, several of his major projects, most notably the final publication of his excavations at Sinda, remained unfinished at the time of his death. Furumark died on October 8, 1982, in Uppsala .

His death did not mark the end of his influence. The systems he created were so embedded in the discipline that they continued to be used, debated, and refined by subsequent generations. The posthumous publication of the Sinda excavations in 2003, completed by his student Charles Adelman and colleague Paul Åström, served as a final tribute to his fieldwork contributions .

## The Furumark System: Analysis and Classification
To understand Furumark’s impact, one must appreciate the chaotic state of Aegean archaeology prior to 1941\. Before Furumark, the dating of Mycenaean pottery was heavily reliant on the system developed by Arthur Evans for Minoan Crete (Early, Middle, and Late Minoan). Scholars like Carl Blegen and Alan Wace had adapted this for the mainland (Late Helladic), but the terminology was often inconsistent, and the distinction between Minoan imports and local Mycenaean products was frequently blurred .

Furumark’s contribution was to treat the pottery not just as art, but as data. He applied a rigid, almost Linnaean taxonomy to the material, breaking down every vessel into two constituent components: Shape and Motif.

### The Furumark Shape (FS)
Furumark created a catalog of all known Mycenaean vessel forms, assigning each a unique number. This system, known as the **Furumark Shape (FS)**, allows archaeologists to refer to specific vessel types with precision, avoiding the ambiguity of descriptive terms like "jug" or "cup" .

The FS system is exhaustive. It covers everything from open vessels like kylikes and craters to closed vessels like stirrup jars and alabastra.

* **FS 171:** A specific type of Stirrup Jar (a vessel used for transporting oil/perfume). 
* **FS 264:** A specific profile of the Kylix (a stemmed drinking goblet). 
* **FS 284:** The Deep Bowl, a shape that becomes diagnostic for the later Mycenaean periods (LH IIIB and LH IIIC) .

By tracking the subtle changes in these shapes over time—such as the gradual elongation of a stem, the swelling of a globular body, or the changing angle of a handle—Furumark was able to establish a relative sequence of development. For example, the profile of the "squat alabastron" (FS 80 vs FS 83\) could indicate a difference between a Late Helladic I dating and a Late Helladic IIA dating .

### The Furumark Motif (FM)
Parallel to the shape analysis, Furumark cataloged the decorative patterns used on the pottery. He identified and numbered over 70 distinct families of motifs, known as the **Furumark Motif (FM)**.2

* **FM 11:** Papyrus. 
* **FM 12:** Sacred Ivy . 
* **FM 21:** Cuttlefish (Octopus). 
* **FM 46:** Running Spiral. 
* **FM 76:** Variegated Stone Pattern .

Furumark’s analysis of motifs was driven by a theory of stylistic evolution. He argued that Mycenaean art began under heavy Minoan influence, characterized by "pictorial" (naturalistic) designs. Over time, the Mycenaean tendency toward order and abstraction caused these naturalistic forms to become "pictorialized" or conventionalized . A lush, growing papyrus plant in LH I might evolve into a stiff, geometric fan shape in LH IIIA, and finally into a simple abstract chevron or line pattern in LH IIIC.

By correlating the evolution of the Shape (FS) with the evolution of the Motif (FM), Furumark created a grid of cross-references that allowed for extremely precise dating. A vessel could be dated not just to a century, but often to a quarter-century based on the intersection of its form and its decoration.

### The Chronological Framework
The practical output of this system was the refinement of the Late Helladic (LH) chronology. Furumark divided the Mycenaean age into granular phases:

* **LH I:** The Shaft Grave period, heavily influenced by Minoan styles. 
* **LH IIA & IIB:** The period of tholos tombs and increasing independence. 
* **LH IIIA1 & IIIA2:** The height of the palatial expansion (e.g., Amarna Age synchronisms). 
* **LH IIIB1 & IIIB2:** The peak and subsequent stress of the palace system (typified by the Zygouries and Granary styles). 
* **LH IIIC:** The post-palatial period.

Furumark’s definition of **LH IIIC** was particularly revolutionary. Prior to his work, the pottery of this period was often dismissed as "sub-Mycenaean" or degenerate. Furumark, following Mackeprang, identified distinct styles within this period, such as the **Close Style** (characterized by dense, busy decoration) and the **Granary Style** (characterized by simple linear bands) . He demonstrated that LH IIIC was a long period with its own internal development, showing cultural continuity rather than the abrupt vacuum suggested by the "Dorian Invasion" theories .

### Critique and Refinement
While monumental, Furumark’s system was not flawless. The primary critique, leveled by scholars such as **Gerald Cadogan** and **Susan Sherratt**, focuses on its "dirigiste" nature .

* **Evolutionary Determinism:** Furumark’s assumption that art always evolves from naturalistic to abstract was criticized as too rigid. Critics pointed out that "revival" styles occurred and that different regions (e.g., the Dodecanese vs. the Argolid) might follow different stylistic trajectories . 
* **Decontextualization:** In his drive for a universal system, Furumark sometimes grouped vessels based on shape/motif without sufficient regard for their archaeological context (stratigraphy). He treated the pottery as an abstract system rather than a product of human agency in specific locations . 
* **Complexity:** The system is notoriously dense. The distinction between a "pictorial" motif and a "pictorialized" one can be subjective, and the sheer number of variations in the MP catalog makes it difficult for non-specialists to use effectively .

Despite these criticisms, the system has proven resilient. Scholars like **Penelope Mountjoy** and **Elizabeth French** have updated Furumark’s work, incorporating new finds from Mycenae and Tiryns to refine the definitions of phases like LH IIIB2 and LH IIIC Middle . However, they retained the FS and FM numbering system, acknowledging that Furumark provided the essential language of the discipline.

## Archaeological Fieldwork
Furumark was not content to remain a purely "armchair" archaeologist. He sought to test his chronologies against the hard evidence of the spade, leading him to conduct excavations in two key regions: Cyprus and Italy.

### The Excavations at Sinda, Cyprus (1947–1948)
In the late 1940s, Furumark was tasked with writing the Late Bronze Age summary for the *Swedish Cyprus Expedition*. He realized that the existing publication record for habitation sites was inadequate to clarify the end of the Bronze Age on the island . He needed a site that would reveal the stratigraphy of the transition from Late Cypriot IIC to IIIA—the era corresponding to the collapse of the Mycenaean palaces.

Site Selection and Excavation: 
Furumark selected Sinda, a site located approximately 20 km east of Nicosia. His interest was piqued by illicit excavations that had brought to light sherds of Mycenaean IIIC1b pottery—a type crucial for synchronizing Cypriot and Aegean chronologies . He conducted excavations over two brief seasons: December 1947 and Spring 1948.4 
Stratigraphy and Findings: 
The excavations at Sinda were highly significant, revealing a fortified town with three distinct phases of occupation during the turbulent years of the 12th century BC 6:

| Phase | Description | Key Finds | Destruction Cause |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Sinda I** | Fortified town with defense system. | Local Cypriot wares, Mycenaean IIIB. | Violent fire (Catastrophe 1\) |
| **Sinda II** | Rebuilt town, new structures. | Mycenaean IIIC1a, Local IIIC1b. | Violent fire (Catastrophe 2\) |
| **Sinda III** | Poorer reoccupation. | Developed IIIC1b ("Close Style"). | Abandonment |

Historical Interpretation: 
Furumark’s interpretation of Sinda was deeply enmeshed in the historical debates regarding the Sea Peoples. He linked the destruction of Sinda I and the subsequent rebuilding in Sinda II (with its influx of Mycenaean IIIC pottery) to the arrival of Greek colonists . He proposed that the first destruction was caused by Greek settlers and the second by the Sea Peoples . 
While modern scholarship has refined the dates (lowering the end of LH IIIB) and often views the "colonization" as a more complex process of acculturation and piracy rather than a single migration event 6, Furumark’s work at Sinda provided the first clear stratigraphic evidence for the presence of Mycenaean IIIC culture in Cyprus. It demonstrated that the island was part of the wider post-palatial Aegean cultural sphere.

Publication Challenges: 
The full publication of Sinda was plagued by delays. Adelman’s preface to the final 2003 volume describes a chaotic archive of "torn plans," "fading negatives," and "incomprehensible field notes" . The site itself was damaged by local villagers in 1951, and many finds stored in the Famagusta Museum were lost during the Turkish invasion of 1974.13 These challenges underscore the importance of the posthumous rescue of this data by Adelman and Åström.

### Excavations at San Giovenale, Italy (1962–1963)
In the 1960s, Furumark turned his attention to the Central Mediterranean. The Swedish Institute in Rome, under the patronage of King Gustaf VI Adolf, began major excavations at **San Giovenale** in Etruria . The site offered a unique opportunity to study the transition from the Bronze Age to the Iron Age in Italy, a period roughly contemporary with the Mycenaean world.

The "Protovillanovan" Problem: 
Prior to the San Giovenale excavations, the "Protovillanovan" culture (the immediate predecessor to the Etruscan Villanovan culture) was poorly understood and often dated to the Early Iron Age. At San Giovenale, Furumark applied his expertise in Aegean ceramics to the indigenous Italian strata. 
Key Discovery: 
In Area D and other sectors, Furumark identified two Mycenaean pottery sherds. He dated these sherds to LH IIIB2–LH IIIC1 (c. 1230–1130 BC) . These sherds were found in association with Protovillanovan material. This was a chronological anchor of immense importance. It allowed the "Protovillanovan" period to be securely dated to the Late Bronze Age (Bronzo Recente), rather than the Iron Age . 
This discovery had ripple effects for Italian prehistory, synchronizing the Italian sequence with the Eastern Mediterranean and supporting the theory of pre-colonial contact between Mycenaeans and Italy. Although later radiocarbon dating at San Giovenale (indicating dates as early as 1420 BC for some layers) introduced new complexities and debates regarding the duration of these phases, Furumark’s ceramic identification remained the linchpin for the relative chronology .

## Theoretical Contributions: Negotiated Positivism
Furumark’s work is often characterized as the pinnacle of "culture-historical" archaeology—obsessed with typologies, lists, and chronologies. However, recent scholarship, such as that by **Johannes Siapkas**, suggests a more nuanced reading of Furumark’s epistemology, describing it as "**Negotiated Positivism**" .

Furumark operated in an intellectual environment that valued scientific objectivity. He believed that archaeology could attain the rigor of the natural sciences through precise classification (hence the FS/FM system). However, he was also a historian who recognized the limitations of archaeological data. In his 1950 work *Några metod- och principfrågor inom arkeologien* (Some Issues of Method and Principle in Archaeology), he grappled with the distinction between "facts" and "interpretations" .

He did not view pottery merely as a tool for dating but as a reflection of the "spirit" of the age. His analysis of the shift from the "naturalistic" art of the Early Mycenaean period to the "formalism" of the Late Mycenaean period was not just a stylistic observation; it was a historical argument about the centralization of power and the rigidification of Mycenaean society . He argued that the "pictorialized" motifs represented a worldview where the content of the representation became secondary to the decorative syntax—a mirror of the bureaucratic palace societies of Mycenae and Pylos.

## Broader Scholarship: Scripts and Religion
### Linear B and the Greek Language
Furumark was one of the first senior archaeologists to fully embrace Michael Ventris’s decipherment of Linear B in 1952\. While some scholars were skeptical that the Mycenaeans could have been Greek speakers, Furumark saw the decipherment as a validation of his own archaeological conclusions regarding the continuity between Mycenaean and later Greek culture .

His 1954 article, "Ägäische Texte in griechischer Sprache" (*Aegean Texts in the Greek Language*), was a pioneering attempt to read and interpret the tablets within their archaeological context . He used the textual evidence to corroborate his ceramic data, looking for correspondence between the administrative regions described in the Pylos tablets and the distribution of specific pottery styles .

### The Settlement at Ialysos
In 1950, Furumark published "The Settlement at Ialysos and Aegean History c. 1550–1400 BC" in *Opuscula Archaeologica*.1 This work was a masterclass in combining settlement archaeology with ceramic analysis. Furumark analyzed the stratigraphy of **Trianda** (Ialysos) on Rhodes, identifying three phases (Trianda I, IIA, IIB) .

He demonstrated that the shift from Trianda I to Trianda IIB represented a transition from Minoan dominance to Mycenaean control in the Dodecanese. This supported his broader historical thesis that the Mycenaeans gradually eclipsed the Minoans not just on the mainland, but throughout the Aegean, eventually taking over the trade routes and political networks of the region . This work challenged the "Pan-Minoanism" of Arthur Evans, who had long argued that sites like Ialysos were merely Minoan colonies. Furumark showed that while they started that way, they became Mycenaean—a distinction made possible only by his precise separation of Minoan and Mycenaean pottery styles.

## Legacy and Impact
The legacy of Arne Furumark is omnipresent in the field of Aegean prehistory. He is one of the few archaeologists whose name has become an adjective; "Furumarkian" is used to describe the standard typological approach to pottery .

### The "Uppsala School" and the Swedish Institute
Furumark was the central figure of the "Uppsala School," a tradition of Swedish archaeology characterized by rigorous typology, a focus on Cyprus and Greece, and a strong engagement with scientific methods . His students, including Paul Åström (who continued the *Swedish Cyprus Expedition* work) and Robin Hägg (who focused on Greek religion), carried his methodologies forward, dominating Swedish classical archaeology for the late 20th century .

### The Survival of the System
The most tangible evidence of his legacy is the continued use of the FS and FM systems. Despite the "New Archaeology" of the 1960s and the "Post-Processual" turn of the 1980s—movements that often rejected the typology-heavy approaches of the past—Furumark’s system survived.

* **Elizabeth French** and the British School at Athens adopted the system for the publication of Mycenae, confirming that Furumark’s sequences (with modifications) held true in the stratified deposits of the Citadel House . 
* **Penelope Mountjoy** published *Mycenaean Decorated Pottery: A Guide to Identification* (1986) and *Regional Mycenaean Decorated Pottery* (1999), works that are essentially user-friendly updates to Furumark. They retain his numbers and his logic, proving that his fundamental insights were sound .

The "Furumark Shape" remains the shorthand for communication. When an archaeologist in Israel finds a Mycenaean sherd and calls it an "FS 36," an archaeologist in Spain knows exactly what is meant. This standardization of language is perhaps the greatest contribution a scholar can make to a discipline.

### Conclusion
Arne Furumark was a scholar of immense intellect and ambition. In an era before computers, he processed vast datasets of ceramic material to construct a chronological system of remarkable durability. His work provided the scaffolding upon which the history of the Aegean Bronze Age has been built. While his specific historical interpretations regarding the Sea Peoples or the exact dates of the phases have been debated and refined, the structure of his thought remains the foundation of the field. As described by the British Academy, subsequent scholars may have adjusted the dates, but they are all "well aware of the analytical approach of the Swedish scholar Arne Furumark... and of the value of Furumark's approach in creating order" . He was, in the truest sense, the architect of Aegean chronology.

Arne Furumark’s contribution was to treat the pottery not just as art, but as data.
Arne Furumark applied a rigid, almost Linnaean taxonomy to the material, breaking down every vessel into two constituent components: Shape and Motif.
Arne Furumark created a catalog of all known Mycenaean vessel forms, assigning each a unique number.
This system, known as the **Furumark Shape (FS)**, allows archaeologists to refer to specific vessel types with precision, avoiding the ambiguity of descriptive terms like "jug" or "cup."
The FS system is exhaustive.
It covers everything from open vessels like kylikes and craters to closed vessels like stirrup jars and alabastra.
FS 171 is a specific type of Stirrup Jar (a vessel used for transporting oil/perfume).
FS 264 is a specific profile of the Kylix (a stemmed drinking goblet).
FS 284, the Deep Bowl, is a shape that becomes diagnostic for the later Mycenaean periods (LH IIIB and LH IIIC).

By tracking the subtle changes in these shapes over time—such as the gradual elongation of a stem, the swelling of a globular body, or the changing angle of a handle—Arne Furumark was able to establish a relative sequence of development.
For example, the profile of the "squat alabastron" (FS 80 vs FS 83) could indicate a difference between a Late Helladic I dating and a Late Helladic IIA dating.
Parallel to the shape analysis, Arne Furumark cataloged the decorative patterns used on the pottery.
Arne Furumark identified and numbered over 70 distinct families of motifs, known as the **Furumark Motif (FM)**.
FM 11 is Papyrus.
FM 12 is Sacred Ivy.
FM 21 is Cuttlefish (Octopus).
FM 46 is Running Spiral.
FM 76 is Variegated Stone Pattern.
Arne Furumark’s analysis of motifs was driven by a theory of stylistic evolution.
Arne Furumark argued that Mycenaean art began under heavy Minoan influence, characterized by "pictorial" (naturalistic) designs.
Over time, the Mycenaean tendency toward order and abstraction caused these naturalistic forms to become "pictorialized" or conventionalized.
A lush, growing papyrus plant in LH I might evolve into a stiff, geometric fan shape in LH IIIA, and finally into a simple abstract chevron or line pattern in LH IIIC.
By correlating the evolution of the Shape (FS) with the evolution of the Motif (FM), Arne Furumark created a grid of cross-references that allowed for extremely precise dating.
A vessel could be dated not just to a century, but often to a quarter-century based on the intersection of its form and its decoration.
The practical output of Arne Furumark's system was the refinement of the Late Helladic (LH) chronology.
Arne Furumark divided the Mycenaean age into granular phases.
LH I is the Shaft Grave period, heavily influenced by Minoan styles.
LH IIA & IIB is the period of tholos tombs and increasing independence.
LH IIIA1 & IIIA2 is the height of the palatial expansion (e.g., Amarna Age synchronisms).
LH IIIB1 & IIIB2 is the peak and subsequent stress of the palace system (typified by the Zygouries and Granary styles).
LH IIIC is the post-palatial period.
Arne Furumark’s definition of **LH IIIC** was particularly revolutionary.
Prior to Arne Furumark's work, the pottery of this period was often dismissed as "sub-Mycenaean" or degenerate.

Arne Furumark, following Mackeprang, identified distinct styles within this period, such as the **Close Style** (characterized by dense, busy decoration) and the **Granary Style** (characterized by simple linear bands).
Arne Furumark demonstrated that LH IIIC was a long period with its own internal development, showing cultural continuity rather than the abrupt vacuum suggested by the "Dorian Invasion" theories.
Arne Furumark's system was not flawless.
The primary critique, leveled by scholars such as **Gerald Cadogan** and **Susan Sherratt**, focuses on Arne Furumark's system's "dirigiste" nature.
Arne Furumark’s assumption that art always evolves from naturalistic to abstract was criticized as too rigid.
Critics pointed out that "revival" styles occurred and that different regions (e.g., the Dodecanese vs. the Argolid) might follow different stylistic trajectories.
In Arne Furumark's drive for a universal system, Arne Furumark sometimes grouped vessels based on shape/motif without sufficient regard for their archaeological context (stratigraphy).
Arne Furumark treated the pottery as an abstract system rather than a product of human agency in specific locations.
Arne Furumark's system is notoriously dense.

The distinction between a "pictorial" motif and a "pictorialized" one can be subjective, and the sheer number of variations in the MP catalog makes it difficult for non-specialists to use effectively.
Despite these criticisms, Arne Furumark's system has proven resilient.

Scholars like **Penelope Mountjoy** and **Elizabeth French** have updated Arne Furumark’s work, incorporating new finds from Mycenae and Tiryns to refine the definitions of phases like LH IIIB2 and LH IIIC Middle.
However, they retained the FS and FM numbering system, acknowledging that Arne Furumark provided the essential language of the discipline.
Arne Furumark was not content to remain a purely "armchair" archaeologist.
Arne Furumark sought to test his chronologies against the hard evidence of the spade, leading him to conduct excavations in two key regions: Cyprus and Italy.
In the late 1940s, Arne Furumark was tasked with writing the Late Bronze Age summary for the *Swedish Cyprus Expedition*.
Arne Furumark realized that the existing publication record for habitation sites was inadequate to clarify the end of the Bronze Age on the island.
Arne Furumark needed a site that would reveal the stratigraphy of the transition from Late Cypriot IIC to IIIA—the era corresponding to the collapse of the Mycenaean palaces.
Arne Furumark selected Sinda, a site located approximately 20 km east of Nicosia.
Arne Furumark's interest was piqued by illicit excavations that had brought to light sherds of Mycenaean IIIC1b pottery—a type crucial for synchronizing Cypriot and Aegean chronologies.
Arne Furumark conducted excavations over two brief seasons: December 1947 and Spring 1948.
The excavations at Sinda were highly significant, revealing a fortified town with three distinct phases of occupation during the turbulent years of the 12th century BC.
Sinda I was a fortified town with a defense system, featuring local Cypriot wares and Mycenaean IIIB, and was destroyed by a violent fire (Catastrophe 1).
Sinda II was a rebuilt town with new structures, featuring Mycenaean IIIC1a and Local IIIC1b, and was destroyed by a violent fire (Catastrophe 2).
Sinda III was a poorer reoccupation, featuring developed IIIC1b ("Close Style"), and was abandoned.
Arne Furumark’s interpretation of Sinda was deeply enmeshed in the historical debates regarding the Sea Peoples.
Arne Furumark linked the destruction of Sinda I and the subsequent rebuilding in Sinda II (with its influx of Mycenaean IIIC pottery) to the arrival of Greek colonists.
Arne Furumark proposed that the first destruction was caused by Greek settlers and the second by the Sea Peoples.

While modern scholarship has refined the dates (lowering the end of LH IIIB) and often views the "colonization" as a more complex process of acculturation and piracy rather than a single migration event, Arne Furumark’s work at Sinda provided the first clear stratigraphic evidence for the presence of Mycenaean IIIC culture in Cyprus.
Arne Furumark's work at Sinda demonstrated that the island was part of the wider post-palatial Aegean cultural sphere.
The full publication of Sinda was plagued by delays.
Adelman’s preface to the final 2003 volume describes a chaotic archive of "torn plans," "fading negatives," and "incomprehensible field notes."
The site itself was damaged by local villagers in 1951, and many finds stored in the Famagusta Museum were lost during the Turkish invasion of 1974.
These challenges underscore the importance of the posthumous rescue of this data by Adelman and Åström.
In the 1960s, Arne Furumark turned his attention to the Central Mediterranean.
The Swedish Institute in Rome, under the patronage of King Gustaf VI Adolf, began major excavations at **San Giovenale** in Etruria.
The site offered a unique opportunity to study the transition from the Bronze Age to the Iron Age in Italy, a period roughly contemporary with the Mycenaean world.
Prior to the San Giovenale excavations, the "Protovillanovan" culture (the immediate predecessor to the Etruscan Villanovan culture) was poorly understood and often dated to the Early Iron Age.
At San Giovenale, Arne Furumark applied his expertise in Aegean ceramics to the indigenous Italian strata.
In Area D and other sectors, Arne Furumark identified two Mycenaean pottery sherds.
Arne Furumark dated these sherds to LH IIIB2–LH IIIC1 (c. 1230–1130 BC).
These sherds were found in association with Protovillanovan material.
This was a chronological anchor of immense importance.
It allowed the "Protovillanovan" period to be securely dated to the Late Bronze Age (Bronzo Recente), rather than the Iron Age.

This discovery had ripple effects for Italian prehistory, synchronizing the Italian sequence with the Eastern Mediterranean and supporting the theory of pre-colonial contact between Mycenaeans and Italy.

Although later radiocarbon dating at San Giovenale (indicating dates as early as 1420 BC for some layers) introduced new complexities and debates regarding the duration of these phases, Arne Furumark’s ceramic identification remained the linchpin for the relative chronology.
Arne Furumark’s work is often characterized as the pinnacle of "culture-historical" archaeology—obsessed with typologies, lists, and chronologies.
Recent scholarship, such as that by **Johannes Siapkas**, suggests a more nuanced reading of Arne Furumark’s epistemology, describing it as "**Negotiated Positivism**."
Arne Furumark operated in an intellectual environment that valued scientific objectivity.
Arne Furumark believed that archaeology could attain the rigor of the natural sciences through precise classification (hence the FS/FM system).
However, Arne Furumark was also a historian who recognized the limitations of archaeological data.

In his 1950 work *Några metod- och principfrågor inom arkeologien* (Some Issues of Method and Principle in Archaeology), Arne Furumark grappled with the distinction between "facts" and "interpretations."
Arne Furumark did not view pottery merely as a tool for dating but as a reflection of the "spirit" of the age.

Arne Furumark's analysis of the shift from the "naturalistic" art of the Early Mycenaean period to the "formalism" of the Late Mycenaean period was not just a stylistic observation; it was a historical argument about the centralization of power and the rigidification of Mycenaean society.

Arne Furumark argued that the "pictorialized" motifs represented a worldview where the content of the representation became secondary to the decorative syntax—a mirror of the bureaucratic palace societies of Mycenae and Pylos.
Arne Furumark was one of the first senior archaeologists to fully embrace Michael Ventris’s decipherment of Linear B in 1952.

While some scholars were skeptical that the Mycenaeans could have been Greek speakers, Arne Furumark saw the decipherment as a validation of his own archaeological conclusions regarding the continuity between Mycenaean and later Greek culture.

Arne Furumark's 1954 article, "Ägäische Texte in griechischer Sprache" (*Aegean Texts in the Greek Language*), was a pioneering attempt to read and interpret the tablets within their archaeological context.

Arne Furumark used the textual evidence to corroborate his ceramic data, looking for correspondence between the administrative regions described in the Pylos tablets and the distribution of specific pottery styles.
In 1950, Arne Furumark published "The Settlement at Ialysos and Aegean History c. 1550–1400 BC" in *Opuscula Archaeologica*.
This work was a masterclass in combining settlement archaeology with ceramic analysis.
Arne Furumark analyzed the stratigraphy of **Trianda** (Ialysos) on Rhodes, identifying three phases (Trianda I, IIA, IIB).
Arne Furumark demonstrated that the shift from Trianda I to Trianda IIB represented a transition from Minoan dominance to Mycenaean control in the Dodecanese.

This supported Arne Furumark's broader historical thesis that the Mycenaeans gradually eclipsed the Minoans not just on the mainland, but throughout the Aegean, eventually taking over the trade routes and political networks of the region.
This work challenged the "Pan-Minoanism" of Arthur Evans, who had long argued that sites like Ialysos were merely Minoan colonies.
Arne Furumark showed that while they started that way, they became Mycenaean—a distinction made possible only by his precise separation of Minoan and Mycenaean pottery styles.
The legacy of Arne Furumark is omnipresent in the field of Aegean prehistory.
Arne Furumark is one of the few archaeologists whose name has become an adjective; "Furumarkian" is used to describe the standard typological approach to pottery.

Arne Furumark was the central figure of the "Uppsala School," a tradition of Swedish archaeology characterized by rigorous typology, a focus on Cyprus and Greece, and a strong engagement with scientific methods.

Arne Furumark's students, including Paul Åström (who continued the *Swedish Cyprus Expedition* work) and Robin Hägg (who focused on Greek religion), carried his methodologies forward, dominating Swedish classical archaeology for the late 20th century.
The most tangible evidence of Arne Furumark's legacy is the continued use of the FS and FM systems.
Despite the "New Archaeology" of the 1960s and the "Post-Processual" turn of the 1980s—movements that often rejected the typology-heavy approaches of the past—Arne Furumark’s system survived.

**Elizabeth French** and the British School at Athens adopted the system for the publication of Mycenae, confirming that Arne Furumark’s sequences (with modifications) held true in the stratified deposits of the Citadel House.

**Penelope Mountjoy** published *Mycenaean Decorated Pottery: A Guide to Identification* (1986) and *Regional Mycenaean Decorated Pottery* (1999), works that are essentially user-friendly updates to Arne Furumark.
They retain Arne Furumark's numbers and his logic, proving that his fundamental insights were sound.
The "Furumark Shape" remains the shorthand for communication.
When an archaeologist in Israel finds a Mycenaean sherd and calls it an "FS 36," an archaeologist in Spain knows exactly what is meant.
This standardization of language is perhaps the greatest contribution a scholar can make to a discipline.
Arne Furumark was a scholar of immense intellect and ambition.
In an era before computers, Arne Furumark processed vast datasets of ceramic material to construct a chronological system of remarkable durability.
Arne Furumark's work provided the scaffolding upon which the history of the Aegean Bronze Age has been built.

While Arne Furumark's specific historical interpretations regarding the Sea Peoples or the exact dates of the phases have been debated and refined, the structure of his thought remains the foundation of the field.

As described by the British Academy, subsequent scholars may have adjusted the dates, but they are all "well aware of the analytical approach of the Swedish scholar Arne Furumark... and of the value of Furumark's approach in creating order."
Arne Furumark was, in the truest sense, the architect of Aegean chronology.

| [![Image 3: Furumark's signature, in a letter of March 1958](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2e/Arne_Furumark_Signature.jpg/250px-Arne_Furumark_Signature.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Arne_Furumark_Signature.jpg) |

**Josef Arne Gerdt Furumark** (26 September 1903 – 8 October 1982) was a Swedish[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAccorinti2014p._323,_n._3-2) archaeologist who specialised in the ceramics of [Mycenaean Greece](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mycenaean_Greece "Mycenaean Greece"). His three-volume work _The Mycenaean Pottery_ established a categorisation and chronology of the ceramics of the [Late Bronze Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Late_Bronze_Age "Late Bronze Age") on the Greek mainland. A 1943 review credited him with doing "for [Mycenaean pottery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mycenaean_pottery "Mycenaean pottery") what [Payne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humfry_Payne "Humfry Payne") did for Corinthian and [Beazley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Beazley "John Beazley") for Attic wares",[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDaniel1943252-3) and subsequent scholars have considered the work a standard reference, though it received criticism for an over-rigid approach and for prioritising stylistic analysis at the expense of information about objects' archaeological contexts.

Furumark was born in the Norwegian capital of [Kristiania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo "Oslo") (now Oslo).[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-Union-1) After an unhappy childhood, in which he initially seemed set to follow his father into the paper business, he entered [Uppsala University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uppsala_University "Uppsala University") in Sweden in 1925 to study the humanities, and became a pupil of the archaeologist [Axel W. Persson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axel_W._Persson "Axel W. Persson"). He obtained his doctorate, with a thesis on the decoration of Mycenaean ceramics, in 1939, and became an associate professor at Uppsala in the same year. He led excavations at [Sinda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sinta,_Cyprus "Sinta, Cyprus") on Cyprus, the first Swedish archaeological work on the island since the [Second World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_World_War "Second World War"), between 1947 and 1948, and became a professor at Uppsala in 1952. He remained there until his retirement in 1970, and served a year's term as director of the [Swedish Institute at Athens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_Institute_at_Athens "Swedish Institute at Athens"), a research centre for classical archaeology, between 1956 and 1957. He also conducted excavations at [San Giovenale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Giovenale "San Giovenale") in Italy between 1962 and 1963, and published on the Mycenaean settlement of the island of [Rhodes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodes "Rhodes").

Although an early sceptic of the idea that the [Linear B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_B "Linear B") script was used to write Greek, Furumark corresponded with [Michael Ventris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Ventris "Michael Ventris"), who deciphered it in 1953, and was one of the first archaeologists to use his conclusion that its language was indeed Greek. Furumark's work on ceramics helped to establish the distinctive nature of mainland Greek ("Helladic") ceramics in relation to Cretan ("[Minoan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minoan_civilization "Minoan civilization")") wares, and highlighted the ways in which both cultural groups influenced each other to varying extents over time. In doing so, he helped to overturn the narrative of [Arthur Evans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Evans "Arthur Evans") that Minoan Crete had dominated mainland Greece throughout the Late Bronze Age. He also established continuity between Mycenaean pottery and that of the following [Protogeometric period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protogeometric_style "Protogeometric style"), and thereby that narratives which argued for the complete overturning of Greek culture at the end of the Bronze Age, such as that of the [Dorian invasion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorian_invasion "Dorian invasion"), were incorrect.

Josef Arne Gerdt Furumark was born on 26 September 1903,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMedwid2000112-4) in the Norwegian capital of [Kristiania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo "Oslo") (now Oslo),[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-5)[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-Union-1) where his father worked as a businessman in the paper industry.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTENylander198334-7) He suffered from a skin condition throughout his life, which left him shy and socially isolated.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTENylander198338-8) Family life during his early years was unhappy; Furumark initially attended business school in Norway and worked in his father's offices in Oslo and in London, where at the age of nineteen he visited the [British Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Museum "British Museum"). He later said that this visit encouraged him to change his studies to archaeology. In 1925, he entered Sweden's [Uppsala University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uppsala_University "Uppsala University"), where he studied a wide [humanities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humanities "Humanities") curriculum including classical archaeology, philosophy and theology. He eventually came to study there under the Mycenaean archaeologist [Axel W. Persson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axel_W._Persson "Axel W. Persson"),[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTENylander198334-7) under whom he took part in excavations in Greece.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTENylander198335-9)

Furumark received his doctorate, with a dissertation on the subject of [Mycenaean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mycenaean_Greece "Mycenaean Greece") ceramic decoration, in 1939. In the same year, he was made an associate professor at Uppsala.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTENylander198335-9) In 1941, he published _The Mycenaean Pottery: Analysis and Classification_ and _The Chronology of Mycenaean Pottery,_[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEH%C3%A4gg1996476-10) a two-volume study which analysed, categorised and dated Late Bronze Age ceramics from the mainland of Greece according to their shapes and decorative motifs.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcDonaldThomas1990300-11) He had begun writing a third volume, _Mycenaean Pottery: A History,_ by 1941, but abandoned the project by 1944.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTESiapkas201814-12) He published _Det äldsta Italien_, a handbook of Italian archaeology, in 1947, which became widely cited: he planned, but never published, an edition in English.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrunnsaker197630-13)

Between 1947 and 1948, Furumark excavated at [Sinda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sinta,_Cyprus "Sinta, Cyprus") on Cyprus.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEH%C3%A4gg1996476-10) Swedish archaeologists had excavated widely on the island before the [Second World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_World_War "Second World War"), but Furumark's was the first Swedish project there after 1945.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStyrenius19948%E2%80%9312-14) The excavation was conducted in two campaigns; the first from 22 December 1947 to 22 January 1948, and the second from 25 March to 7 May 1948.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFurumark200363-15)[Carl-Gustaf Styrenius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl-Gustaf_Styrenius "Carl-Gustaf Styrenius") later credited Furumark's excavations with expanding scholarly knowledge of migration from Greece to Cyprus at the end of the Bronze Age.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStyrenius199412-16) The project uncovered a [Late Cypriot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Late_Cypriot "Late Cypriot") (c. 1300– c. 1200 BCE) settlement with [Cyclopean walls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyclopean_masonry "Cyclopean masonry"),[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEG%C3%B6ransson2012419-17) though only excavated a small fraction of its total area of around 46,500 square metres (11.5 acres).[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEIacovou200710-18) In 1948, during a visit to the Bronze Age site of [Hala Sultan Tekke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hala_Sultan_Tekke_(archaeological_site) "Hala Sultan Tekke (archaeological site)") on the island, he noticed a large [pithos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pithos "Pithos") in a field, which prompted new excavations around it.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTE%C3%85str%C3%B6m1978232-19)

In 1950, Furumark argued, on the basis of the ceramics of Minoan Crete, that the idea of the Cretan site of [Knossos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knossos "Knossos") being ruled by Greek-speakers in the Late Minoan II period (c. 1490– c. 1430 BCE) was "untenable":[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-20) the fact of mainland rule over Crete in this period was established two years later by [the discovery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decipherment_of_Linear_B "Decipherment of Linear B") by [Michael Ventris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Ventris "Michael Ventris") that the [Linear B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_B "Linear B") tablets made there at this time were written in a form of Greek.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcDonaldThomas1990314-21) Furumark had maintained a correspondence with Ventris since 1951;[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHedlund200310-22) after Ventris proposed his decipherment, Furumark worked with [Gudmund Björck](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Gudmund_Bj%C3%B6rck&action=edit&redlink=1 "Gudmund Björck (page does not exist)")([sv](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gudmund_Bj%C3%B6rck "sv:Gudmund Björck")), the professor of Greek at Uppsala, to check its accuracy. The two wrote to Ventris in October 1952 to give their verdict that he was correct.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHedlund200311-23)[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-25) Furumark was one of the first archaeologists to use his decipherment in his own work.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-ArtHistDict-26)[[c]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-28) Also in 1950, he argued that Mycenaean settlers had arrived on the island of [Rhodes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodes "Rhodes") around the turn of the Late Helladic IIB and IIIA periods (that is, c. 1400 BCE), that they lived peacefully alongside the pre-existing population, who used [Minoan pottery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minoan_pottery "Minoan pottery"), and were allowed to live in existing houses. Mario Benzi, in 1988, called this idea "astonishing", and suggested that the Mycenaean incomers more probably subjugated the inhabitants by force.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBenzi198859-29)

Furumark became Professor of Classical Archaeology and Ancient History at [Uppsala University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uppsala_University "Uppsala University") in 1952,[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEH%C3%A4gg1996476Medwid2000112-30) succeeding Persson.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTE%C3%85str%C3%B6m20037-31) In the early years of his professorship, he was involved in reorganising the university's collection of antiquities,[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTENylander198335-9) and created a small museum in two of the university's rooms.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrunnsaker197631-32) He served as director of the [Swedish Institute at Athens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_Institute_at_Athens "Swedish Institute at Athens"), a research centre for classical archaeology, between 1956 and 1957.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAccorinti2014p._323,_n._3-2) Among his students at Uppsala were [Margareta Lindgren](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Margareta_Lindgren&action=edit&redlink=1 "Margareta Lindgren (page does not exist)"), who worked on Linear B,[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTENoschEnegren2017xxviii-33) and [Gisela Walberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Gisela_Walberg&action=edit&redlink=1 "Gisela Walberg (page does not exist)"), who extended his work on Mycenaean ceramics to those of [Middle Minoan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Minoan "Middle Minoan") Crete,[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHood1978375-34) as well as [Sture Brunnsåker](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sture_Brunns%C3%A5ker&action=edit&redlink=1 "Sture Brunnsåker (page does not exist)")([sv](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sture_Brunns%C3%A5ker "sv:Sture Brunnsåker")) and [Carl Nylander](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Carl_Nylander&action=edit&redlink=1 "Carl Nylander (page does not exist)")([sv](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Nylander "sv:Carl Nylander")).[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrunnsaker197631-32) His own academic work during his professorship, in contrast to his previous studies of Mycenaean and Italian archaeology, focused on the ancient Aegean scripts.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrunnsaker197630%E2%80%9331-35) In 1956, he gave a lecture in Berlin in which he attempted to decipher the [Linear A](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_A "Linear A") tablets uncovered at the site of [Hagia Triada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hagia_Triada "Hagia Triada") on Crete,[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacKendrick1981120-36) using the methods applied by Ventris to Linear B,[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBraidwoodMason195859-37) and posited that Linear A had similarities with the Anatolian [Indo-European language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indo-European_languages "Indo-European languages") of [Luwian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luwian_language "Luwian language").[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacKendrick1981120-36)[[d]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-39) He was appointed a member of the [Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Swedish_Academy_of_Sciences "Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences") in 1958.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPohl1958412-40) Between 1962 and 1963, he excavated at [San Giovenale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Giovenale "San Giovenale") in Italy,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEH%C3%A4gg1996476-10) continuing excavations begun there in the 1950s by the [Swedish Institute in Rome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_Institute_in_Rome "Swedish Institute in Rome").[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKarlsson200622-41) After recovering from a period of serious illness in the late 1960s,[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTENylander198335-9) he retired from his professorship in 1970,[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEH%C3%A4gg1996476Medwid2000112-30) and was succeeded by his former student Sture Brunnsåker.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrunnsaker197631-32) He died on 8 October 1982 in Uppsala.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMedwid2000112-4)

Contributions to archaeology
----------------------------

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Arne_Furumark&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Contributions to archaeology")]

[![Image 4: Goblet-shaped ceramic vessel, with a tall stem and two handles, painted in black with a squid design](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/19/Cup_squid_1300-1200_BC_Staatliche_Antikensammlungen.jpg/250px-Cup_squid_1300-1200_BC_Staatliche_Antikensammlungen.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Cup_squid_1300-1200_BC_Staatliche_Antikensammlungen.jpg)

Mycenaean [kylix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kylix "Kylix") of the Late Helladic IIIB period

Johannes Siapkas, in 2022, identified Furumark as part of a Swedish tradition, traceable back to the work of [Erik Hedén](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Erik_Hed%C3%A9n&action=edit&redlink=1 "Erik Hedén (page does not exist)")([sv](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erik_Hed%C3%A9n "sv:Erik Hedén")) at the turn of the twentieth century, to distinguish the academic treatment of the ancient world from the popular understanding of it, and to prioritise scientific objectivity in its reconstruction.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTESiapkas2022114-42) A 1943 review of _The Mycenaean Pottery_ credited him with doing "for Mycenaean pottery what [Payne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humfry_Payne "Humfry Payne") did for Corinthian and [Beazley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Beazley "John Beazley") for Attic wares";[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDaniel1943252-3) Siapkas compared his work with that of [Johann Joachim Winckelmann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johann_Joachim_Winckelmann "Johann Joachim Winckelmann") on ancient sculpture.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTESiapkas20187-43)

_The Mycenaean Pottery_ was the first complete survey of its subject published in book form,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcDonaldThomas1990300-11) and became the established point of departure for subsequent studies.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTESiapkas20187-43) Furumark's approach developed from that of German stylistic analysis, known as _Strukturforschung_ ('Structural Research'), first practised in the 1920s by archaeologists such as [Friedrich Matz](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Friedrich_Matz_(born_1890)&action=edit&redlink=1 "Friedrich Matz (born 1890) (page does not exist)")([de](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friedrich_Matz_der_J%C3%BCngere "de:Friedrich Matz der Jüngere")).[[e]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-45) However, Furumark rejected the association made in _Strukturforschung_, under the influence of [Nazi racial theories](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazi_racial_theories "Nazi racial theories"), between cultural styles and biological races.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTESiapkas201815-46) As well as ceramic vessels, he named and categorised the terracotta figurines known as [psi, phi, and tau types](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psi,_phi_and_tau_type_figurine "Psi, phi and tau type figurine").[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench1971103-47) The archaeologist [Robin Hägg](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Robin_H%C3%A4gg&action=edit&redlink=1 "Robin Hägg (page does not exist)")([sv](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin_H%C3%A4gg_(arkeolog) "sv:Robin Hägg (arkeolog)")) described the books as Furumark's "_magnum opus_ ... [and] ever since the standard work on this topic";[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEH%C3%A4gg1996476-10) Linda Medwid called them "the definitive reference on the subject" in 2000.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMedwid2000113-48) Although the [absolute dates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Absolute_dating "Absolute dating") of Furumark's chronology have generally been revised, the categories and reference he assigned to particular shapes and motifs remain conventional vocabulary within the field.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTESherratt2011258-49)

Furumark's contemporary [Alan Wace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Wace "Alan Wace") criticised him for what he called "excessive [pigeonholing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pigeonholing "Pigeonholing")" of ceramic styles, and for ignoring information about the archaeological contexts in which finds were unearthed; the latter criticism was also articulated by Wace's collaborator [Carl Blegen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Blegen "Carl Blegen").[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTESiapkas20187-43)[Susan Sherratt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Susan_Sherratt "Susan Sherratt"), in 2021, criticised Furumark's approach as "essentially stylistically based and unrealistically over-analytical", particularly by contrast with that of [Lisa French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_French "Elizabeth French"), who worked on Mycenaean pottery in the second half of the twentieth century.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTESherratt2021-50)[Gerald Cadogan](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Gerald_Cadogan_(archaeologist)&action=edit&redlink=1 "Gerald Cadogan (archaeologist) (page does not exist)") described Furumark's approach as _[dirigiste](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirigiste "Dirigiste")_ for what he considered its excessive devotion to ordered categorisation.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTECadogan2003353-51)[[f]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-53) Sherratt elsewhere criticised Furumark's system for lumping together variations of shape and motif into single categories, on the basis of what he considered to be evolutionary relationships between them.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTESherratt2011258-49) She also disagreed with his treatment of individual motifs and shapes in isolation, rather than as part of coherent decorative schemes.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTESherratt2011259-54)

### Influence on Minoan and Mycenaean studies

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Arne_Furumark&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Influence on Minoan and Mycenaean studies")]

[![Image 5: Tall, wide-necked vessel decorated with a simple geometric drawing of a chariot.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/78/Amphoroid_krater_with_chariot_scene%2C_1300-1250_BC%2C_AM_of_Nafplio%2C_202188.jpg/250px-Amphoroid_krater_with_chariot_scene%2C_1300-1250_BC%2C_AM_of_Nafplio%2C_202188.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Amphoroid_krater_with_chariot_scene,_1300-1250_BC,_AM_of_Nafplio,_202188.jpg)

Mycenaean [krater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krater "Krater") from the Late Helladic IIIC period, as defined by Furumark

[![Image 6: Vessel decorated with simple geometric drawings of horses.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/24/Horses_manger_Louvre_A513.jpg/250px-Horses_manger_Louvre_A513.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Horses_manger_Louvre_A513.jpg)

Furumark argued that the ceramics of the [Mycenaean civilisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mycenaean_civilisation "Mycenaean civilisation") of mainland Greece were a development of pre-Mycenaean mainland forms, with influence from contemporary Minoan Crete.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMedwid2000112-4) This aligned with the view set forth by Wace and Blegen in 1918, that the civilisation of mainland Greece had been broadly continuous and indigenous throughout the Bronze Age. This view, known as the "Helladic Heresy" ("Helladic" meaning "native to mainland Greece"),[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWaceBlegen1918118%E2%80%93119Galanakis2007241-55) was itself an extension of the archaeological theory of [Christos Tsountas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christos_Tsountas "Christos Tsountas"), who argued for the continuity of Greek culture from prehistory to the modern period.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPliatsika2020292-56) Furumark established the sub-periods of the [Helladic chronology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helladic_chronology "Helladic chronology") based on the stages of development of pottery styles, which became the standard [relative chronology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Relative_dating "Relative dating") system used in studies of the Mycenaean period.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcDonaldThomas1990300-11)

Furumark's findings contradicted the idea of [Arthur Evans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Evans "Arthur Evans"), who had named Minoan civilisation in the early 20th century, that Mycenaean civilisation had developed from that of Crete.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMedwid2000113Galanakis2007240-57) Furumark concluded that the level of Minoan influence in mainland ceramics changed over time, with an overall balance roughly even between Cretan- and indigenous-derived vessel shapes, a high level of Cretan influence in the Late Helladic IIIA period (c. 1400– c. 1300 BCE), and a dominant mainland influence in the following Late Helladic IIIIB period (c. 1300– c. 1180 BCE).[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-58) He therefore rejected both the term "Late Minoan", used for mainland pottery of the Late Bronze Age by Evans and [Duncan Mackenzie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duncan_Mackenzie "Duncan Mackenzie"),[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcDonaldThomas1990300-11) and Wace and Blegen's "Helladic", which he considered to imply that developments on the mainland were isolated from the wider Aegean. Since Furumark's work, the terms "Helladic" and "Mycenaean" have been considered equivalent,[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMedwid2000113-48) though his belief that "Helladic" did not adequately encompass the influence of Crete and the other Aegean islands has generally been rejected by other scholars.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcDonaldThomas1990300-11)

Medwid called _The Mycenaean Pottery_ "a final refutation" of Evans's view that Mycenaean Greece had been subordinate to Minoan Crete, referencing Furumark's demonstration of the continuity of Mycenaean pottery as well as that certain Mycenaean forms, such as the [kylix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kylix "Kylix"), were adopted on Crete.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMedwid2000113-48) Following the 1938 work of Mogens B. Mackeprang,[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-59) Furumark included two styles of pottery, found by Wace at Mycenae and labelled by him the Granary Style and the Close Style, in his categorisation of the Late Helladic IIIC period (c. 1180– c. 1050 BCE).[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-60) He identified a trend in the later part of the period towards simple geometric designs,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcDonaldThomas1990300-11) establishing continuity between Mycenaean pottery and that of the following [Protogeometric period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protogeometric_style "Protogeometric style"), and thereby that narratives which argued for complete cultural collapse or replacement at the end of the Bronze Age, such as that of the [Dorian invasion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorian_invasion "Dorian invasion"), were incorrect.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMedwid2000113-48)

Description
-----------

When Arne Furumark was entrusted with writing the Late Bronze Age summary volume for the Swedish Cyprus Expedition, he realized that a habitation site was needed in order to clarify problems associated with the last phases of that period. As neither the French nor the Cypriote excavations at Enkomi had yet been published he decided to find his own site: he scouted several, but settled on Sinda because recent illicit digging there had thrown up sherds of a sort never before seen on the Island, namely Mycenaean IIIC1b. He conducted two short excavation seasons but the control excavation he planned was aborted when he received notice from the Cypriote authorities that there was large scale destruction of the site. Although there is evidence of earlier and later habitation at Sinda, the most important is the Late Bronze Age fortified town (probably built along the copper trading route), with its three phases: Sinda I, II, and III.

Sinda I, which saw the building of the defense system and had a material culture including local Cypriote wares as well as examples of Mycenaean IIIB, suffered major destruction. Sinda II followed: Structures were repaired and built, and were accompanied by a rich material culture including Mycenaean IIIC1a and great quantities of locally produced, early IIIC1b materials. A second catastrophe brought an end to that town. Sinda III followed, a poorer town, but with examples of locally produced, developed IIIC1b wares of the Close Style. Furumark's interpretation that the two destructions were brought about first by Greek settlers and then by Sea Peoples has been challenged by more recent archaeological evidence which lowers the date of Mycenaean IIIB. Paul Astrom, in his summary suggests a reasonable alternative, that pirates and adventurers were responsible for the destructions. -- Provided by publisher

MYCENAEAN LERNA  

> (PLATES

17-3 1)  

> T

HE EXCAVATION OF ANCIENT LERNA, south of the village ofMyloi, on the west shore of 

the Argive Gulf, was conducted between 1952 and 1958 under the general direction of 

John L. Caskey, then Director of the American School of Classical Studies at Athens.' The My-

cenaean finds from Lerna are stored in the Archaeological Museum at Argos. A few of them are on 

display in the exhibition room devoted to Lerna. Most of the records on the Lerna excavations are 

kept at Dartmouth College; some, including photocopies, are kept in Argos or at the American 

School of Classical Studies at Athens. 

The site of Lerna (Fig. 1) was occupied continuously from Early Neolithic times into the Late 

Bronze Age. The general appearance of the area in the Late Bronze Age, after extensive erosion 

and consequent deposition of alluvium in the eastern part of the plain during the Early Helladic 

(EH) period, seems to be little changed today. At that time, however, the shallow Lake Lerna 

existed to the north of the site, and the seacoast lay closer to the site of Tiryns.2 

Evidence for the Mycenaean occupation of Lerna (Lerna VII), after the period of the Lerna 

shaft graves (Lerna VI), comes chiefly from the trenches in Area D on the northeastern side of 

the mound, in an area measuring roughly twenty meters by ten meters. The work here was begun 

in 1952 with a trial trench and continued with more extensive excavation in 1953 and 1954. The 

center of the mound had been heavily eroded and its post-Middle Helladic (MH) strata largely 

lost, aside from the two shaft graves and other burials of that period.3 (t should be noted that 

only about one-seventh of the entire surface of the mound was excavated.) Trial trench C, just 

northwest of the main area and high in the center of the mound, produced a few Late Helladic 

(LH) I-II sherds in disturbed surface lots4 but nothing later. Grave DE-1 of early LH IIB, in 

Area DE, reflected the LH II presence, and clear strata in trench F, below the LH IIIB 1 horse 

burial, were datable to LH IIA-B. It is sufficiently clear that there was some kind of continuing 

activity at the site from Middle Helladic times into the Late Helladic period, but in LH IIIAI 

it may have been rather slight. Very few sherds that are clearly LH IIIAI have been recovered  

> l

To Professor John L. Caskey, Director of the Lerna Excavations, I owe a large debt of thanks. From the time 

he invited me as a student to join the excavation staff until his early death, he encouraged me with unfailing patience and 

advice. Tucker Blackburn supplied every need, from photographic expertise to editorial direction. Members of the 

Lerna staff contributed much: S. Charitonides, Epimelete in the Department of Antiquities in the 1950s; Elizabeth G. 

Caskey, excavator; Helen Vasileiou Buck and Aliki Halepa Bikaki, the original trench masters of Area D, and Elizabeth 

Courtney Banks, who followed them and summarized their work; Elizabeth McLeod, who wrote up a survey of the 

Mycenaean material and kindly allowed me to use it; and Lloyd Cotsen, architect of the plans. I want also to thank Sarah 

Rutter, who inked most of the pottery drawings; Julia Pfaf, for the new general plan, Fig. 1; Gatewood Overbeck, who 

wrote a preliminary catalogue of the figurines; Jeremy Rutter, Carol Zerner, and Karen Foster, for their helpful advice; 

Curtis Runnels, for comments on the chipped stone here cited; the Athenian Agora Excavations, for the developing and 

printing of many of the photographs, most of which were taken byJ. L. Caskey; the American School of Classical Studies 

at Athens and its directors, past and present, especiallyJames R. McCredie and William D. E. Coulson, for much help; 

the staffofthe Publications office ofthe School; the Ephors ofAntiquities for the Argolid, especially Photeini Pachygianni; 

and the staffs, past and present, of the Corinth and Argos museums and the site of Lerna, for countless helpful acts. I owe 

many thanks also to the American Council of Learned Societies, for a fellowship that supported my work in 1977, to the 

staff of the Humanities Computer Center at Dartmouth College, for much assistance, and to the Classics Department of 

Dartmouth College, for making available space for the storage and use of Lerna research material.

(P385-P388, fill deposit 7, and P473 and P478 in trench F), an indication perhaps of a low 

population at this time. 

The Mycenaean deposits in Area D, at the edge of the mound, lay at a level not much 

higher than that of the much older EH II House of the Tiles to the southwest. Even so, little of 

the LH IIIA2-B1 Mycenaean settlement survived here. It succeeded a MH settlement without 

evidence for intervening occupation, aside from scattered sherds. At some point within LH I1IA2 a

filling operation was undertaken, presumably in order to correct the unevenness of the ground 

occupied in Middle Helladic times and to prepare it for occupation by a growing population. Earth 

containing sherds from earlier constructions elsewhere was brought in to form fill deposit 7. Two 

LH IIIA2 burials, graves D-2 and D-10, were placed here, probably before the new construction 

began; the great slab of D- 10 (Plate 20:b) may have stood as a monument when the earlier floor 

in Area 5 was laid down, but D-2, a child's grave east of Area 5, may have been forgotten before the 

walls nearby were set. Room 1 and its main floor, and the walls west of it, were constructed within 

late LH IIIA2; Area 5, with its lower floor, was perhaps laid out at the same time or slightly later. 

The builders of Room 1 employed a line of MH wall foundations still standing at its southeastern 

corner, and a MH street to the south continued to be used. Occupation of the main floor of 

Room 1, and also of the lower paving in Area 5, ended within early LH IIIB 1. A second partial 

floor in Room 1 indicates a scant reoccupation there. A deposit on a more extensive floor in Area 5

is certainly datable to early LH IIIB 1. No higher, or later, LH strata were preserved in this area, 

but mixed surface deposits here and elsewhere on the site produced a few sherds of LH 111B2 date. 

Beyond Area D the Mycenaean occupation is seen to the south in trench F, where the burial of 

a horse, possibly to be associated with a human grave, is datable to LH IIIB I.5 Farther to the west, 

also on the lower slopes of the mound, another grave (K-1) is probably of LH 111A2 date.6 Here the 

underlying strata were of Lerna IV, the latest Early Helladic period. 

The pottery catalogued below represents the bulk of the Mycenaean ceramics excavated at 

Lerna. Some 200 other, less diagnostic sherds are kept in the museum in Argos. The surviving 

material was decreased by early discards, both at the site and in preparation for final storage in 

Argos, where space was limited. Most decorated pottery was retained, but most coarse sherds and 

less diagnostic unpainted sherds were not kept. Absolute proportions of pottery classes therefore 

cannot be extracted from the present material, but it is unlikely that anything of substantial 

chronological significance has been lost. 

Most of the pottery is of the ordinary fine Mycenaean fabric (no grits larger than 2 mm). 

Coarse pottery is so described. Undecorated ware, if not coarse, is either of "standard" (porous 

surface) or "polished" type.7 Unless otherwise stated, the Lerna pottery is "polished," a type 

formerly called "slipped." The colors of the fabric and paint of Mycenaean pottery are well known 

and are recorded here, using Munsell terminology,8 only for certain significant vessels. Where 

possible, shapes and decoration are identified according to the system devised by Arne Furumark,9 

with modifications by Penelope Mountjoy. 10 All vessels are wheelmade unless otherwise indicated. 

Pottery is numbered P1, P2, and so forth, in sequence as described, and other objects as 

MOl, M02, and so forth. The pottery lot numbers mentioned are those that were assigned 

during the course of excavation. The walls are numbered in sequence (W-1, W-2, and so forth), 

and the room deposits are numbered according to the first wall in the room (e.g., Room 1 from wall 

W-1), with deposits numbered similarly (e.g., deposit 7 from wall W-7).

> 6Caskey 1955, p. 47.
> 7The distinctions are those of Wardle (1969, p. 281).

The small objects include quite a number and variety of terracotta figurines and a group of 

unusual faience beads from grave D-2. There is not much metal, aside from lead pottery clamps, 

and tools are of stone or bone, with terracotta whorls for spinning and more elegant steatite 

whorls perhaps for dress weights." 1 Two obsidian arrowheads suggest hunting, perhaps of the deer 

recorded among the fauna. The faunal remains include the usual types: Sus, Capra/Ovis, Bos, Lepus, 

Canas, and Cervus, as well as Equus caballus in trench E 12 

The following abbreviations are used: CR = descriptions of chipped stone furnished by 

Curtis Runnels; FM = Furumark motif and FS = Furumark shape;'3 Gejvall = unpublished notes 

by Nils-Gustaf Gejvall in the Lerna archives. All measurements are in meters unless otherwise 

indicated.
