# 2.2. The Swedish take 

Swedish scholars first encountered the term Protovillanova while excavating San Giovenale. 

In the begi nn ing, older material s, now called Protovillanova, was classified as Early Iron Age, 

or Early Villanova. This was later corrected and the term Protovillanova was used to describe 

the Bronze Age pottery from San Giovenale. In the 1960’s , Swedish scholars believed that the 

Protov illanova cultural phenomeno n was a result of an isolated Apennine culture heritage 

with Villanova influences. This led to Swedish scholars becoming convinced that there was a 

clear distinction between Protovillanov a and Bro nzo Finale an d that Protovillanov a should be 

treated as a culture rather than a time sequence. 

Furthermore, a few Swedish scholars question ed the traditional dating of the 

Protovillanova and that it should not be classed as a culture active duri ng Bronzo Finale but 

rather during Bro nzo Recente. 40 The reason for questioning the dating of the period had to do 

with two carbon -14 samples taken from House III, Room B in Area F East of San Giovenale ,

in a layer of clay that was found directly over the bedrock. 41 In the layer of clay, a large 

amo unt of charcoal from a hearth was uncovered and tested. 42 The two tested examples were 

of high quality and the results were considered to be 100% safe. The two calibrated dates for 

the Pr otovillanova layer were between 1420 –1210 and 1450 –1370 BC with a 68 .2% accuracy 

and 1510 –1110 and 1500 –1310 BC with 95 .4% accuracy .43 

Besides the two carbon -dated tests, there is yet one more factor to account for. In Area D 

of San Giovenale, in an un identified context, scholars discover ed two Mycenaean pottery 

sherd s.44 Th e sherd s were dated to LHIIIB2 -LHIIIC1 by Arne Furumark. 45 

# 2.3. Problematizing the term Protovillanova 

At the end of the Final Bronze Age, all over central and some northern areas , the region s went 

through a landscape reconstruction. 46 Small settlements were either abandoned or became 

larger settlements or proto -urban cities. Therefore , it is not always so that an area sh ould have 

traces of both Protovillanova and Villanova. In the case of San Giovenale, there are some few 

Villanovan sherds, but (for now) the re is no strong Villanova presence. 47 

When researching the Protovillanova cultures , it is vital to understand that the Bronzo 

Finale period had innovating te ndencies and could include regional pottery expressions that

# 3. Analysis of the biconical jar s 

> Fig. 2. Anatomy of the biconical jar.

The following analysi s is based on the biconic al jar sherds found in the three boxes of pottery 

from Luni and the fourteen boxes of pottery from San Giovenale. The sherds from Luni and 

San Giovenale are mixed between published and unpublished sherds. 

The decoration patterns are categorised and then co mpared to other biconical jars from 

various site s in central and northern Italy . This will be done in order to place the sherds in to a

cultural context. The sherds are categorized according to the decorati ve pattern on them. The 

sherds will be described an d compared to the categorization system Barbaro has created for 

the Bronzo Finale pottery. The pattern decoration that Barbaro has created will be used to date 

the decoration patterns t hat have been found in San Gio venale and Luni. After categorizing 

the decorations , a comparative section will compare the decorations from San Giovenale and 

Luni with the decorations found in various areas in central and northern Italy that are 

categorized a s either Bronzo Finale or P rotovillanova .

For this thesis, only the decoration patterns will be analysed. The reason for not including 

manufactural methods, fabrics, surface treatments, colour and sizes is simply that there is not 

room enough for such a discussion in this thesis. 

The Biconical jar s from San Giovenale and Luni are found in settlement context s, and are 

therefore not burial urns but rather storage vessels. 

In the physical material there are no complete biconical jars but there are a couple of 15 

examples of more or less entire vessels in the publications from both San Giovenale and 

Luni. 51 

# 3.1. Biconical jar s from San Giovenale and Luni 

The standard form of th e biconical jar from San Giovenale and Luni consist of a neck, 

shoulder and body (Fig. 2 ). The biconical jar has an equally long neck as the body. However ,

there are examples of vessels with either a longer neck or a longer body. The shoulder is 

rather sha rp as it is the merging point for the neck and body. The vessel has a straight conical 

neck. The neck and the body are commonly in a sharp angle creating a “diamond” form for 

the vessel: t he biconical jar is described as two cones put together . The biconical jar has either 

a slightly everted rim or an everted rim with a flattened top. During the Bronzo Finale and/or 

Protovillanova period it can vary slightl y from region to region and from vessel to vessel. 

The biconical jar can be both used as a st orage unit but also as a burial urn. Therefore, it 

can be found in necropoleis as well as in settlements. The various sites discussed later in this 

chapter inclu de both necropoleis and settlements. The difference between the burial urn and 

the jar is that the urn has an upside -down placed bowl as a lid, in order to protect the ash and 

bones of the cremated individual. 

3.1.1. Decoration pattern on biconical jar s fr om San Giovenale and Luni 

There are altogether 20 different decoration patterns from San Giovenale and Luni (Fig. 3 –

4). The most common pattern is the incised lines, both horizontal and diagonal. The incised 

lines can either be created with a comb or wit h a sharp object such as a needle. The 

characterisation of the decorations made with a comb is that the incised lines becomes evenly

not . The dimples are presumably created from the simple push from a fi nger and a small sharp

# 3.2. Comparison 

In this se ction the decoration patterns on the biconical jars from San Giovenale and Luni are 

analysed and compared to those from various sites in central and northern Italy . The biconical 

jars are in most cases classified as Bronzo Finale. There are some few exampl es of biconical 

jars classified as Protovillanova, and these will be included in the comparison. The aim of the 

comparison is to see if there are differentiations between the two site s’ biconical decoration 

patterns and if there is any correlation to the o ther sites in central and northern Italy classified 

as Bronzo Finale. 

Decoration patterns on potteries have through our modern times been a tool for dating or 

used as proof of a time period. The decoration pattern on the biconical jar is no ex ception. I n

Barbaros publication over the biconical jar decoration pattern s are not only categor ized into 

different periods of Bronzo Finale but are then in turn used to date archaeological s ites and 

chronological layers. The Bronzo Finale with simple patterns is in Barbaros publication dated 

to be Bronzo Finale I, the more intricate the pattern becomes the later the dating is as it slowly 

transcends into becoming a Villanovan pattern. The dat ing that Barbaro has created for the 

patterns is convincible as it follows a clear pattern of pattern development.

There are some few complete (or nearly complete ) biconical jars in the publications of San 

Giovenale and Luni. From San Giovenale there are two nearly complete biconical jars, one 

from Karlsson ’s publication ,107 and one from Pohl’s publication .108 For Luni there are three 

re constructed biconical jars: t wo in Hellström ’s publication ,109 , and the third in Wieselgren’s 

publication .110 All the almost comp lete biconical jars were found in a settlement context. 

What is essential to note is that there are two vessels with a rather interesting and unique 

decoratio n combination. The biconical jar s with the unique pattern is included are found in 

Wieselgrens and Karlssons publication .111 The uniq ueness lies in the fact that a fluted rim that 

circles around the entire shoulder of the vessel , in combination with a B P1 patter n with 

impressed dimples above the incised lines, except for an impressed dimple on the unders ide, 

tucked in to the corner of the up side -down V-formation. The incised line s with impressed 

dimples are reminiscent of the decoration type M111 in Barbaro’s publication. 112 In 

comparison , Barbaro does not include any examples of such a decoration combinatio n. 

Although there are no further examples of this decoration combination in Barbaro’s 

publication, a version of the co mbination of this pattern seems to appear in other Bronzo 

Finale areas of central and northern Italy , as well as in the archaeological mat erial culture 

group To lfa -Allumiere . There are altogether four examples from Sorgenti della Nova. 113 The 

fi rst two examples for comparison are publishe d by Dolfini and Passoni, have the same 

combination of oblique fluting and B P1 decoration pattern . Both ves sels ar e categorized as 

Bronzo Finale . H owever , example fig. 2, no. 1 is also categorized as belong ing to the 

Allumiere -phase of the Bronzo Finale III .114 Example fig 2, no.1 is more rounded in the form ,

compared to both the San Giovenale and Luni’s example s, and was found in either a funerary 

context or a settlement context .115 Example fig. 3 has both the fo rm and decoration 

combination seen in the vessels from Luni and San Giovenale. 116 The example fig. 3 was 

found in a settlement context, to be precise, withi n the wal ls of an o val hut. 

There are two more examples , published by Cassano and Manfredini, that I would like to 

compare to the San Giovenale and Luni biconical jar s with the unique pattern. Both examples 

are categorized as Protovillanovan and their d ecoration pattern combination varie s slightly 

compared to the examples from San Giovenale and Luni . Exampl e fig. 7 , no. 5117 has a light 

oblique fluting on the shoulder, just as the Luni and San Giovenale vessel s, but has instead a 

combination of B P13 and B P16 decoration patterns over the oblique fluting. The form is 

however the same as the two examples from San G iovenale and Luni . Example fig. 7, no. 5 is 

found in a settlement context from Torrionaccio. As for exa mple B1 ,118 it has a similar 

combination to exa mples fig. 2, no. 1 and fig. 3 but lacks the impressed dimples. The example 

is classified as late Protovillanovan of the Allumiere group and where it was found is not

There seems therefore that there are no indication that the oblique flutin g would appear 

only on funerary biconical jars (biconical urns) , but seems to be a decoration combination also 

used in the settlement, such as houseware or storage units . As for the example fig. 2, no.1 ,

which is categorized as Bronzo Finale III , this coul d point to the fact that the claimed 

Protovillanova sites of San Giovenale and Luni continued into the late stages of the period. 

The claim that the last two examples, fig. 7, no. 5 and B1 , are Protovillanovan stems from the 

fact that both published works are from the 1960’s and 70’s, when using that term had not yet 

become controversial. 

Although there are some similarities between the decoration patterns on the potter y from 

Luni and San Giovenale , there are differences between the representation of what decoration 

pattern can be found in Luni and San Giovenale . There are altogether eight exa mple pairs of 

decoration patterns from San Giovenale/Luni that have comparisons to sherds with similar 

decoration patterns from various sites in northern and central Italy. The eight example pairs 

will be compared w ith Barbaro’s classifications .

(1) The first decoration pattern that can be found in both Luni and San Giovenale is the 

BP9 decoration pattern . The pattern has horizontal incised lines and a row of small impressed 

dots , either over or under the rows of incised horizontal lines. In the previous section , the B P9

was compare d to Barbaro’s M36 (Table 2 ). However, the sherds of BP 9 do not show the 

complete decoration pattern and it is uncertain whether there we re two rows of impressed 

dots. Thus, the decoration type can also be M37. 120 But as there is only one row visible , it 

should be categorized based on what can be seen and not guessed. According to Barbaro’s 

categorization, this decoration was common in the la st phase of Bronzo Finale (Bronzo Finale 

III) , giving us an example from the later phase from Luni and San Giovenale . The horizontal 

incised lines that are visible on all the sherds from B P9 are presumably created with a comb, 

as the lines are evenly space d out between each other. There are fourteen examples from 

various areas in central and northern Italy that correlates to the BP9 decoration pattern . The 

eight sherds are, however, much like the sherds of B P9, fragmentary and do not always show 

the entire decorati ve pattern . Example fig. 3, no, 2 is from Isola Farnese 121 and is categorized 

as Protovillanova n and shows only parts of the decoration . The decoration pattern consists of, 

much like the BP 9, horizontal lines and a row of impressed dots. 122 The impress ed dots on 

example fig.3, no. 2 are slightly more irregular compared to the B P9 sherds. The decoration 

pattern seems to have been situated on the neck of the biconical jar. 

Example fig. 45, no. 7A and fig. 60, no. 8 are from La Civita ,123 and are categoriz ed as 

Bronzo Finale pottery. E xample fig. 45, no. 7A does not show , like the B P9 , the entirety of 

the pattern ,124 while example fig. 60, no. 8 does show more than just a section of the pattern. 

There is one entire lane of impressed dots and above are several horizontal incised lines. 125 

The pattern on example fig. 60, no. 8 shows that it is very likely that there only existed one 

row of impressed dots, instead of two rows. 

There are several examples from is from the necropol eis of Villa del Barone ,126 

categori zed as Protovillanova pottery. Example s fig. 44, no s. o – p, fig. 50, nos d – e, fig.52, 

nos. j – o consist of many small sherds with incised lines and dots .127 However, fig. 50, nos. d 

– e does not only consist of one row of impressed dots and horizontal i ncised lines , but has 

two rows of impressed dots on some of the examples sherds . Example fig. 52, nos. j – o

include, much like fig. 50, nos. d – e, a second row of impressed dots.

The B P9 decoration pattern is, according to the examples brought up in this section, are 

not unique and can be fou nd in both Bronzo Finale and Protovillanova classed pottery. 

(2) The BP6 decoration pattern can be f ound in both Luni and San Giovenale. There 

are six sherds from San Giovenale and three from Luni. There are between four and eight 

incised lines on the sherds BJ14 – BJ19 . All the sherds have, except BJ15 complete 

decoration pattern, wich means that all th e incised lines in the pattern are visible. The t hree 

sherds BJ20 – BJ22 have five to seven horizontal incised lines. The incised lines on both B P6 

are made with a co mb. The decoration pattern on the biconical jars would be set on the neck, 

above the shoul der. The B P6 decoration pattern correlate well with Barbaro’s M34. 132 

According to Barbaro’s categorization system the decoration would have been common 

during Bronzo Finale I, II and III .133 

Before comparing the B P6 to other biconical jars ’ decorati on patte rns categorised as 

Bronzo Finale, it is vital to understand that the sherds from Luni and San Giovenale are not 

complete, meaning that the pattern is not complete unless there the biconical jar is whole. The 

pattern coul d therefore have been vertical or di ago nal rather than horizontal. The reason for 

establishing the incised lines as horizontal is because there are examples from both Luni and 

San Giovenale that suggest that the lines were horizontally placed , such as sherds BJ14, BJ19 

and BJ20.

(3) The BP8 decoration pattern can be found in both San Giovenale and Luni . There are 

three sherds from Luni ( BJ35 – BJ37 ) and two from San Giovenale (BJ33 – BJ34 ). The BJ36 

is the only sherd that doe s not show the V formation, as the other two sherds do. However, 

there are small indication s, barely visible , that point to another row of incised line s. All sherds 

have an impressed dimple situated in the crevasse of the V formation. The incised lines are 

evenly spa ced and made with a comb. None of the sh erds from BP8 ha ve a complete pattern. 

The B P8 correlate well with Barbaro’s M87 and places the decoration in Bronzo Finale III .140 

The decoration pattern would be situated on the neck, ov er th e shoulder or on the shou lder of 

the biconical jar. 

The re are two examples with correlat ing patterns to the BP8 . The first e xample , fig. 1, is 

from Montebello Vicentino ,141 and is categorised as Bronzo Finale II .142 Example fig. 1 

includes four horizontal incised lines above the zigz ag pattern. The inclusion of the inc ised 

lines sets it apart from the B P8. The decoration pattern is more complete in comparison to the 

decorations found on the sherds from B P8 , as the entire vessel of the biconical jar is sketched. 

The second e xample , f ig. 105, no. 4, is from Orte and categorised as Bronzo Finale. 143 

The example , much like the sherds of B P8 , is fragmentary and onl y shows the diagona l

incised lines that make up the visible zigzag pattern, together with the impressed dimple that 

is placed in the crevasse of the V -form . The pattern of example fig. 105, no. 4 is located on 

the sh oulder of the biconical vessel. 

Besides these two examples there is one further example that should be brought up. The 

ex ample is not a sherd per se, but an early cat egorization of the decoration pattern. In an 

article written by Paola Ucelli Gnesutta, 144 the decoration pattern is classified as a typical 

Protovillanova decoration .145 The decoration pattern w as found on several sherds of biconical 

jars while excavating the settlement at Sor genti della Nova in 1974 –1977. The decoration has 

a striking similarity to the B P8 decoration paterns , with no horizontal incised line s as example 

fig. 1 has. 146 On both the decoration pattern example s, example fig. 1 and Barbaro’s M87 

there are several imp ressed dimpl es, both over and under the zigzag pattern. As all the sherds 

of B P8 show s only one impressed dimple, the assumption is made that there must been more 

to the decoration pattern . It is, however, not clear and therefore the assump tion should not be 

made whether the fragment had any horizontal incised lines over or under the zigzag patt ern.

# 4. Analysis of the zoomorphic handle from San Giovenale and 

# Luni     

> Fig. 5.Anatomy of the zoomorphic handle.

The following analysis is based on the three boxes of mixed pottery from Luni and fourteen 

boxes of mixed pottery from San Giovenale . In this analysis , only the zoomorphic handle will 

be presented and analysed. The zoomorphic handle is the handle type that is most common on 

the carinated bowl or cup from San Giovenale and Luni . The handle is connected at two 

points to the carinated cup or bowl (Fig. 5 ). The first connection is at the shoulder o r carina of 

the ca rinated bowl/cup and acts as the base of the handle. The second connection point works 

as a support beam for the handle and connec ted to the rim of the carinated bowl/cup and at the 

midpoint of the high swung loop handle. At the top of the high swung loop handle there is a 

zoom orphic head, portraying a ewe ’s or a ram ’s head. 205 However, there are some rare cases 

where the zoomorp hic heads are referred to as a duck ’s head 206 or as a horse ’s head. 207 

The head is always situated facing the inside o f the bowl and the loop is facing the outside 

of the carinated bowl or cup. The loop handle is never decorated, but there are some examples 

that have impressed dimples on the base of the loop handle. The decorations that can be found

bowl. The complete form of the handle is elliptical. The “head” of the zoomorphic handle has 

two small protruding “horns” or “ears” , one on each side. Each ear /horn can be decorated with 

two to four incised lines. From the head, a protruding comb reaches from the forehead down 

to the base of the handle, attaching to the vessel’s shoulder (Fig. 5 ). The “comb” makes out 

for the outside the handle. From the head a neck , that then transcends into a chest, reaches 

down and is attached to the rim of the carinated bowl or cup. 

In order to accurately portray t he individual zoomorphic handle s in this thesis, they will 

be divided according to the patterns that are visible , in order to present each difference

exceptions ). The chapter will first present the zoomorphic handles f rom San Giovenale and 

Luni , and wi ll be conclude d with a comparative section , where the zoomorphic handles from 

San Giovenale and Luni will be compared to other zoomorphic handles from various areas of 

central and northern Italy. 

4.1.1. Zoomorphic handles from San Giovenale and Luni 

In t his section , the zoomorphic handles from San Giovenale and Luni will be categorised 

according to decoration that ca n be found on them . There are altogether eleven pattern types 

on zoomorphic handles from S an Giovenale and Luni ( Fig. 6 ). Altogether there ar e 40 

handles. Eight handles are from Luni and 31 handles from San Giovenale 41

Decoration pattern ZP1 (9:1a -2b )

The ZP1 (Fig. 6 ) is a high -sw ung loop handle with a zoomorphic top, and in some cases, there 

is a support between the back, flattened stem and the carinated cup/bowl . The neck is narrow 

and broadens at the chest. The zoomorphic top or head has pointed horns /ears on each side 

and the n ose is e ither rounded o r cylindrical. The decoration for the Z P1 handle consists of 

horizontal incised lines and impressed dimples. The incised lines stretch from the neck down 

to the chest. The impressed dots are placed after the incised lines at the base of the handle and 

on t he inside of the vessel ( ZH1 ). The handle ZH1 is complete with an entire zoomorphic 

head, ears /horns, flattened back stem and support. The handle in ZH2 is not as complete . The 

handle in ZH1 has a complete zoomorphic head, with ears/ horns, back stem and su pportive 

stem and has a smaller part of the rim attached. In Karlsson’s publication there is one 

zoomorphic handle with Z P1 patter n.208 The resemblance of the pattern and the location of the 

pattern on the zoomorphic handle makes it a close match. Both hand les are from San

# 4.2. Compariso n

In this section a comparison will be presented between the zoomorphic handles from San 

Giov enale /Luni and various sites in central and northern Italy . The aim of the com parison is 

to see if there are any similarities between the decoration patterns . These comparisons cover 

zoomorphic handles that have been categorised as either Protovillanova or Bronzo Finale. 

Before delving into the similarities, an issue must be brought up: the lack of published 

zoomorphic handles. Th e cause could be for two reasons : that there are simply not many 

zoomorph ic handles outs ide of San Giovenale and Luni or that the handles have si mply been 

prioritised away in light of other pottery forms. Although the re is a lack of published 

zoomorphic handles with a ram/ ewe ’s head , there are other zoomorphic handles from oth er 

region s in Italy with different portrayals of animals, such as duck, bull or snail. 220 Both the 

duck and the snail zoomorphic handles do however occur both during the Bronzo Recente and 

Bronzo Finale period. 221 The bull handles are however classified as Bro nzo Rece nte as most 

zoomorphic bull handles are from the Terramare region and culture. 222 Much like the 

zoomorphic ram/ ewe ’s head the portrayals of the duck, bull or snail are not always given, but 

are rather anthropomorphic and symbolic. The zoomorphic snai l and duck, however, might be 

more a term that modern scholars have used to explain the form of the zoomorphic handle 

rather than portraying these two animals. Whereas the zoomorphic bull has a stronger 

indication of portraying a bull, because of the clear ly desi gned bull horns.

# 5. Discussion 

Below is a discussion on whether the pottery from San Giovenale and Luni can be 

characteristic as Protovillanovan or Bronzo Finale or eve n both. The section will also include 

a discussion on the dating from San Giovenale. 

5. 1. The mixed dat ing of Protovillanova 

To start the discussion whether or not the pottery material from San Giovenale and Luni 

should be classified as Protovillanova or Bronzo Finale, one must take into account , one 

cross -dating and two radiocarbon lab tests from the so ca lled Protovillanovan layer of San 

Giovenale. 

The cross dating is based on two Mycenean sherd s found in 1958 in Area D of San 

Giovenale. The first sher d was created in purified and light brown clay with the remains of a 

painted black spiral on the surface , while the second is created in a purified yellow clay with 

no decoration but a handle. 239 The sherds were found in an unidentified Bronze Age layer and 

was dated by Arne Furumark to LHIIIB2 –LHIIIC1. The sherds are therefore dated between 

1230 and 1130 BC. Th e Mycenean sherds were therefore used to date the Protovillanovan 

layer . Besides the issues that the sherd was found in a mixed and top layer context one must 

add that the sherds were presumably not made in San Giovenale and would possibly have 

traveled from far away . Therefore, a sure dating based entirely on the sherds is not possible .

The second dating are two carbon -14 tests , taken from a layer o f clay above the bed rock 

under House III in Area F E ast of San Giovenale. The charcoal was f ound in a hearth together 

with i mpasto sherds. Two sample s were taken and tested in 2000 and 2005. The first sample 

came back with a 68.4% probability, with the two calibrated dates of 1420 –1210 and 1450 –

1370 BC. The second sample came back with a 95.4% probability, with two calibrated dates 

of 1510 –1110 and 1500 –1310 BC. According to the diagrams, 240 the dating s would most 

likely fall between 1400 –1200 BC . The dates p oint ed to a much earlier period of 

Protovillanova than previously thought. According to the Ångström ’s Laboratory in Uppsala, 

the samples were of highest quality and the results should therefor e be 100% safe. However, 

the 100% is for the charcoal that was found in the hearth but not for the actual hearth. The 

charcoal could therefore be from wood much older than the date of the actual hearth. 

However, the tests have been used to argue that the Protovillanova culture in San Giovenale 

was active during Bronzo Recente rather than Bronzo Finale. If we continue on the thought 

that Protovillanova was incorrectly dated from the start and that it was active during Bronzo 

Recente rather than Bronzo Finale, would this hypothesis even be possible? And could one 

see Br onzo Recente characteristics in the material from San Giovenale and Luni? The answer 

is both a yes and no . For although there are some similarities between the zoomorphic handles 

from San Giovenale and Luni to the Bronzo Recente pottery, th ere are fa r more similarities 

with the Bronzo Finale for the biconical jars . To con clude, most decoration patterns on the 

biconical jar are categorized as Bronzo Finale III , according to Barbaro’s categorization. 

Com pared to the zoomorphic handles, there are no deco ration types on the biconical jar that

5.2. Protovillanova vs. Bronzo Finale and Bronzo Recente 

An important note in discussing whether to use the term P rotovillanova is that the 

class ification is nearly identical with the Bronzo Finale pottery and therefore become s two 

separate classifications of the same phenomena. The term Protovillanova has an 

archaeological historical hypothesis while Bronzo Finale st ems from an archaeological 

reality. 241 The archaeological reality being that termino logy and labels can be conventional ,

all depending on the context, time and author. The connecting factor for both Bronzo Finale 

and Protovillan ova is the concept of a “proto -Villanovan ” phenomena as a premise of the Iron 

Age civilization . Swedish scholars , compared to the Italian scholars , were careful and would 

often use later dates rather than early. 242 Further, the usage of the term Protovillanova was to 

formulate the transi tion between Bronze Age and Iron Age. However, somewhere along the 

way, the meani ng of Protovillanova became lost and replaced, turning it into a time period, a 

culture or a phenomenon . What this thesis has shown is that it all depends on the Bronze Age 

or Protovillanovan material . By only concentrating on the b iconical jar s, there would be no 

need to have a coined term for the decoration or form, and there would definitely not be 

enough to consider Protovillanova as a culture, neither a phenomenon. The ter m would be 

excessive to say the least, for most decoration patterns fou nd on the biconical jars of San 

Giovenale and Luni are found in the categorization of decorations classified as Bronzo Finale. 

However , it does become much more complex when including t he zoomorphic handles. 

The zoomorphic handles, in comparison to the biconic al jars, lack published examples 

from other regions than San Giovenale and Luni. There are only a few published zoomorphic 

handle s and most of them are undecorated. The lack of z oomorphic handles could also point 

to something more exciting, for you see most biconica l jars are found in necropoleis and not 

in settlement context, in comparison to San Giovenale and Luni. However , the zoomorphic 

handle seems to have stayed clear from the necropol eis and were only foun d in settlements. 

Because of this, one would imagin e that the difference did not lie in a cultural expression but 

rather in what kind of pottery was used in a funerary /burial context verses a settlement 

context .

As for t he zoomorphic handles, as mentioned above, there are a few other examples from 

other settlements than Luni and San Giovenale. However, t hose found are not decorated to the 

same extravagant elegance that can be found on the ha ndles of San Giovenale and Luni .

Could this therefore be a sign that San Giovenale and Luni are distinguished in comparison to 

the others and could this be a sign of a cultural expression rather than a period ? Can scholars 

really define the zoomorphic handles to be a new cultura l expres sion completely different 

compared to other Bronzo Finale settlements and is therefore worthy of being classified as 

Protovillanova rather than the time period Bronzo Finale ? If we are to continue with the

I therefore s uggest that the usage of the term Protovill anova should either be abandoned ,

# 6. Conclusion : To be or not to be Protovillanova? 

The material for this thesis consisted of : 40 biconical sherds from San Giovenale, 17 biconical 

sherds from Luni, 26 zoomorphic handles from San Giovenale and 6 zoomorphic handles 

from Luni. The decoration patterns on the biconical sherds and zoomorph ic handles were then 

meticulously studied and categorized. The biconical sherds were divided depending on if they 

were divided into pattern categories, according to the decoration pattern on t hem . Altogether 

33 pattern categories were created. 20 pattern categories for the biconical sherds from San 

Giovenale and Luni and 13 pattern categories for the zoomorphic handles from San Giovenale 

and Luni. The pattern categories were then compared to other biconical jar decorations and 

zoomorphic handles from variou s archaeological sites in northern and central Italy. The 

comparison material for the biconical jars from San Giovenale and Luni were classified as 

Bronzo Finale or Protovillanova. The comparison material for t he zoomorphic handles from 

San Giovenale and L uni were classified as Bronzo Finale, Protovillanova and Bronzo 

Recente. In order to deduce if the term Protovillanova was usable and if the pottery material 

from San Giovenale and Luni were to be classified as Protovillanovan, Bronzo Finale or 

Bronzo Rece nte, a literature study was made on what Italian and Swedish scholars h ave 

written about the term Protovillanova. 

In conclusion the answers that I have found are quite straight forward. To start with; does 

the term Protovillanova intend to express a per iod of time, much like Bronzo Finale, Bronzo 

Recente and Iron Age or does it intend to name a cultural expression of a civilization. The 

answer is that the term is supposed to express a cultural phenomenon for a region. 

Unfortunately, the region seems to i nclude most of northern and central Italy, and 

furthermore, the term is also used on settlements that does and does not have a strong 

Villanovan presence. Because of the large area it covers and that the term is used for claimed 

Protovillanova settlements that have or do not have a Villanovan heritage, I argue that the 

term is only explaining the same phenomenon as the term Bronzo Finale. Despite the carbon -

14 dating from the “Protovillanovan” layer of San Giovenale, I will argue that there is no 

decoration pattern that comes close enough to the decoration patterns found in San Giovenale 

or Luni (or any other “Protovillanovan”/Bronzo Finale site) to strengthe n the claim that the 

pottery could be Bronzo Recente rather than Bronzo Finale. 

The claimed Protov illanova pottery of San Giovenale and Luni is reclassified as Bronzo 

Finale because of the statement made above. San Giovenale and Luni do not express a 

sp ecific cultural expression, even though there are plenty of zoomorphic handles in both 

areas, but whi ch are rarely found at other sites. My argument is that the zoomorphic handles 

(from San Giovenale and Luni) do not mark a cultural expression that differs from Bronzo 

Finale materials at other sites, but rather indicates a lack of published materials and an 

obsession from scholars to excavate necropoleis rather than settlements. Furthermore, it the 

zoomorphic handles could be a Bronzo Finale expression only found in settlements rather 

than necropoleis. Both biconical jars and zoomorphic handles suggest tha t both Luni and San 

Giovenale had an active settlement during Bronzo Finale III. There are some few pottery 

sherds and handles that suggest that Luni might have had some activity during Bronzo Finale 

I, and that both Luni and San Giovenale might have had s ome activity during Bronzo Finale 

II. 

Furthermore, I would argue that the zoomorphic handles portray either an ewe or a ram, 

depending on if the horns/e ars have incised lines. With incised lines they might portray a ram 

while those without incised lines might portray a n ewe. However, this claim needs to be 

backed up by the not yet published osteological material from San Giovenale , as the 60 

osteological mat erial could confirm, depending on the species of sheep or goat, if both the 

ewe and ram had horns or if it solely is the ram that can grow horns. 

I therefore propose that the term “Protovillanova” should not be used unless it is 

rebranded as a term for a regional pottery expression. However, even if the last suggestion 

might seem reasonable , it is imp ortant to recognize that all regional pottery expressions 

cannot be given names. So, for the time being, I suggest that scholars stay clear from using 

the term Protovillanova .61

The pottery and figurines from the Mycenaean cemeteries at Kolonaki, Hagia Anna, Ismenion and Elektrae Gates in Thebes were first published by the excavator A. Keramopoullos in the AE 49 (1910) and AD 3 (1917) in association with the chamber tombs and also in context with the other tomb deposits. These early studies provide information on the condition in which the tombs and their context were discovered and also give detailed information of the locus of the burial deposits. In some cases, comparisons are drawn with materials from other Mycenaean sites and, in general, there is an occasional discussion of the antiquity or the lateness of the shapes and decorative themes. Observations on burial practices are frequently made. The pottery from these cemeteries was used by A. Furumark in his study of the Mycenaean pottery classification, and since then it has entered the studies of Mycenaean pottery as compara-tive material. In recent years, Mycenaean Boeotia is undergoing a renaissance with the rescue excavation in Thebes carried out by the Archaeological Service, the systematic excavations at Gla undertaken by the Archaeological Society at Athens and the publication of old collections from Boeotian Myce-naean levels. The time was ripe for a re-examination of the pottery and the figurines from the Keramopoullos excavations. Only the vases that were made available, which is the great majority of the material appear at the catalogue of this publication while the pottery which has been entered in the Museum of Thebes Catalogue has been considered in the discussion. A few specimens were omitted by the cataloguer from the Museum Catalogue; thus we were unable to util -ize the descriptions for those vases which could not be located. While pottery that was not examined by us was not included in the catalogue, there is one exception, item MTh 460, because of its recent publication with good documentation. This decision was made in order to keep mis-takes of identification to a minimum. 14 MYCENAEAN POTTERY AND FIGURINES KERAMOPOULLOS EXCAVATIONS The information derived from descriptions in the original publica-tions has been incorporated into the commentary. The descriptions in our catalogue are brief and in accordance with the format established by A. Furumark. The commentary is primarily an analytic discussion of the shapes and decoration of each vessel, followed by comparisons with similar vases from other sites and with the appropriate bibliography. The figurines are discussed within their typological grouping and in a format similar to the one applied for the pottery. Some taphonomical observations on the Theban Mycenaean burials were made at the end, based on Keramopoullos’ and more recent excav-ations. I am thankful for this publication to Dr A. ## OBSERVATIONS ON POTTERY Jars Three-handled (Myc. IIA - Myc. IIIA:1-2) The earliest three-handled jars from the tombs at Kolonaki, Hagia Anna and Ismenion date in the Myc. IIA (cat. nos 1-8). The shapes represented are: FS 20 (cat. nos 1-4), FS 21 (cat. nos 5-7) and FS 24 (cat. no 8). The conical-piriform (cat. nos 1-4) is medium size; cat. no 1 has a straight neck, grooved handles, and torus base, all of which are painted. Against a dotted background is the ivy FM 12x, with cross inside, FM 54 (3), rock patterns FM 32 I (10), and pendant FM 38 (6). There is clarity and fine organization of the patterns. Very similar to this is the jar from Kolonaki tomb 26, MTh 426, which is pictured in ΑD 3 (1917) 200, fig. 144 (1) without comment. Cat.no 3 has splaying neck, grooved handles and splaying base, all of which are painted. The ivy, FM 12v, is against a dotted background void of other themes. The band which connects the ivy has some similarity with a Kakovatos jar 1 . Very similar to this group is also the jar from Thorikos 2. Cat.no 2 has splaying neck and foot and grooved handles, all of which are painted. The decorative zigzag design, FM 61 (14), is rare and when it appears, on later pottery, it is limited only to parts of the vase; it could be a derivative from the clusters of parallel vertical lines. Cat. no 4 has a concave neck, splaying base and grooved handles; they are all painted. The dominant decorative motive is the ogival canopy, FM 13 (1), “starfish”, FM 26 (3), and joining semi-circles, FM 42 (3); dotted lines ran along the canopies and also surround the “starfish”. The conical jars, FS 21 (cat. nos 5-7), were found one at each of the three cemeteries: Kolonaki, Hagia Anna and Ismenion, and all three are medium size vases. Cat. no 5 has concave-splaying neck, oval-flattened handle and splaying base, all painted. The running spiral, FM 46 (12), is a very common motif which appears on a variety of vases and it is widely spread 3. Cat. no 5 has been misidentified as alabastron 4. IIIB-C) The two collar-necked jars, cat. nos 24-25, are undecorated, domestic wares. Cat. no 24 has slightly spreading neck, flattened handles which rise from the middle of the neck, and a raised base. It is FS 67 and ranges from Myc. IIIB-C. Similar but larger than cat. no 24 is known from a house at Mycenae 36 , cat. no 25 is a coarse ware jar with one handle miss-ing. It is a storage jar, FS 66, with a short neck, round handles and a raised base. As most domestic wares range chronologically rather widely. MTh 653, published by Keramopoullos 37 , comes from t. 25 at Kolonaki; it is a medium size jar, 0.25m in height, similar to cat. no 25; it could not be located at the Museum. Another jar, listed by Furumark as found in t. 21 at Kolonaki 38 , is probably from t. 19 39 .Jugs Beaked (Myc. IIB - Myc. IIIA:1) The beaked jugs from Kolonaki (cat. nos 26, 27, 30) and Ismenion (cat. nos 28, 29) cemeteries span between Myc. IIB and Myc. IIIA: 1. They are large, high quality vases. The earliest examples are cat. no 26 from tomb 14 and cat. no 27 from tomb 26 at Kolonaki. Cat. no 26 is FS 143 of the depressed ovoid form with a long cut-off beak; it has a neck moulding of the intermediate type (ring), arched ridged handle, and raised base. Handle and base are painted. The foliate band at the base of the neck, FM 64 (9), the scale on the neck, FM 70 (46) and the argonaut design, FM 22 (4) are Myc. IIB common themes. The Theban specimen is prob-ably the most elegant of its type; other examples are known from the Argolid, Attica, Thessaly and the Dodecanese 40 . It has been reconstructed and one of the argonauts, which were missing in part, has been painted in non-attested finial. An identical vase was found at Iolkos 41 , and Prosy -mna 42 . Shards with small foliate motif were found in Kolonaki t. 3, pos-sibly from a jar or jug. Cat. no 27 has the neck and handle restored after cat. no 26, which it resembles very closely in the ovoid shape and dec-oration. The raised base is angular. It is decorated with a free zigzag motif, FM 61 (2), on the base of the neck and an argonaut on the belly, which is a version of FM 22 (6); the replacement of the argonaut shell 43. Cat. no 38 is the lower part from a stirrup jug with torus base and has been decorated with bands 47 . Cat. no 34 is pictured, in the original publication, along with the preserved bottom of cat. no 38. Cat. no 32 is piriform, FS 150, with two spouts, one more prorounded and cut-off and the other shorter and rounded; the handles are round and arched. Spout, neck and lower half of the body are decorated with bands; the handles are painted; a single dotted line on the shoulder, FM 41 (6), and a scale pattern, FM 70 (1), on the upper half of the body complete the decor-ation. MTh 484 describes a stirrup jug from Kolonaki t. 14 of the same shape and size as cat. no 32, undecorated; it was not located at the Mu-seum. Cat. no 33 is piriform, FS 150, with rather short cut-off spout, round sloping handles, and torus hollowed base. The handles are placed slightly off the diametric line. The lower part above the base is painted, and the spout, neck, handles and most of the body, with the exception of the shoulder zone, are decorated with bands. Papyrus motif with curved stem, FM 11 (47), fills the shoulder area. Cat. no 35 is heavily restored at the lower half so that its attribution to FS 150 is not secure; it has two spouts and handles similar to cat. no 32, and it is undecorated. Cat. no 36 is advanced piriform, FS 151, characteristic of the late phase of the Myc. IIIA: 2. The spouts are minimally formed, the handles are round and rather arched, and the base is torus-disc type. A ledge moulding very close to the base of the neck resembles the Myc. IIIB type. Handles and foot are painted; the neck and the body at its diameter and above the foot are decorated with bands; a diaper net pattern, FM 57 (2), covers the shoulder region. Cat. no 37 is also an advanced piriform stir-rup jug with one spout cut off and the second one rounded and shorter; it resembles cat. no 32. The handles are round and arched, and the base is splaying; the neck has ledge moulding. It is undecorated. OBSERVATIONS ON FIGURINES Most of the figurines found at the Kolonaki and Ismenion cemeteries at Thebes are females of the Phi, Tau and Psi types; one is a kourotrophos. A few represent animals, mainly bovine, and thrones of the types with solid and latticed back; a human figure is seated at one of the thrones with a solid back. A reexamination of these finds was considered appropriate after recent excavations in Boeotia, the publication of the Orchomenos old materials, and the study of the clay figurines by E. French some years ago 216 . Systematic and rescue excavations have produced a consid-erable number of the already known types, and new locations of figurines’ discovery, since the publication by E. French, have become known 217 .Thirty-nine figures are listed in the Museum Catalogue, and five more were found uncatalogued amongst the materials from Keramopoullos’ ex-cavations at Kolonaki and Ismenion. In the report, published in AD 3(1917) thirty-four figurines from Ismenion tomb 2 and Kolonaki tombs 1, 6, 14, 16, 17, 21 and 25 are mentioned. Phi type It seems that there is only one Phi figurine, cat. no 143, of the advanced Phi style from Kolonaki t. 1, dated in the end of Myc. IIIA, which agrees with the date of the pottery from this tomb. Cat. no 143 does not wear a polos, the hair bulges though outwards and it is painted with some detail. Polos is rare in Phi figurines 218 , the closest to Thebes’ example being the one from Zeli Lokris 219 . Hankey refers to four figurines of this type from Thebes, but does not indicate their location 220 . The rarity of the Phi type is probably accidental; neighbouring Orchomenos has produced several Proto-Phi, PhiA and PhiB 221 , and also at least fifteen Phi type from the Tanagra cemetery are exhibited at the Museum of Thebes 222 . A bovine with unusual decoration, cat. no 180, comes from t. 25; it combines the linear type with semicir-cles. There are no other animals identical in decoration. The date of cat. no 180 and, possibly, of cat. no 181, also from t. 25, is Myc. IIIB. The figurine cat. no 182, from t. 21, comes from a IIIA context. Thrones All four thrones were found in t. 25. Cat. no 183 is a type A with a seated figurine 260 . Type A was popular at Tanagra, from where two examples with seated figurines are exhibited at the Museum in Thebes. The seated figurine, of the Theban example, cat. no 183, is barely distin guishable from the back of the seat, and its breasts are made in a very low relief. The upper body is painted with vertical lines and the lower with hori-zontal lines, suggesting possibly folded legs. The “penmanship” of the decoration is similar to the lines on the bodies of the bovine figu rines from the same tomb, which would date throne cat. no 41 within the same Myc. IIIB period of the animal figurines. Cat. nos 184-185 are of the latticed shape, type B, without seated figurine. These are the only known examples from Boeotia; the other region which has produced very simi-lar thrones is the Argolid 261 . It is possible that the Boeotian type B thrones were imported from the Argolid. Cat. no 186 is a type A without a seated figurine. The wing-like projections are rare. The large number of type A thrones found in Boeotia, and especially at Tanagra, may sug-gest a center of production, Argolid being the other center. In conclusion: The terracotta figurines from the cemeteries at Isme-nion and Kolonaki are chronologically clustered around the late Myc. IIIA and early to middle Myc. IIIB. They represent the female figurine varieties known from this period, with the exception of Proto-Phi, which is lacking here. There is a limited variety in animal figurines, and a small number of thrones. The context of the tombs does not support expressed suggestions that the figurines were associated with children’s burials. They have been found with children’s and adult’s burials alike. Certain aspects of the Myc. IIIB figurines are lacking from the Kolonaki and Ismenion cemeteries in Thebes, such as combinations of two or more figurines, or the indication of painted jewelry on the females. On the other hand, the exactness of the similarities in the execution com-pared with figurines found in Boeotia but also in Attica and the Argolid ―such as the presence of the miniature type, the polos, or the horizontal lines of the backs of hair to indicate braids― point to the Mycenaean Koine rather than a local Theban workshop. 56 MYCENAEAN POTTERY AND FIGURINES KERAMOPOULLOS EXCAVATIONS CONCLUSIONS The pottery from the Mycenaean cemeteries of Kolonaki, Hagia Anna, Ismenion and Elektrae Gates in Thebes provides the dates and length of time during which the chamber tombs were used (Table I), provides information on what kind of activities were related to the burials in Mycenaean Thebes, and also shows the types of form (Tables II-V) and decorative motifs (Table VI) that were popular within each phase of the Mycenaean period. The latter information places Thebes in context within the rest of the Mycenaean world. The conclusions are based primarily on a) the material that was avail-able for study at the Museum of Thebes, b) the information extracted from the Museum Catalogue, and c) the re-evaluation of the original excavation report and references made on the tombs materials, by the excavator, Furumark, and other scholars. In the tables, which compute the pottery shapes and motifs, information is taken from the Museum of Thebes Catalogue, the original excavation report, and other published references which are asterisked. Kolonaki is the larger of the Mycenaean cemeteries in Thebes; six-teen of the twenty-eight chamber tombs produced 175 vases, a few of which were found in parts; 175 have been catalogued, but several could not be located at the facilities of the Museum of Thebes. Large crates, where some of these finds might be, could not be reached. The period during which each tomb was in use is assumed to be the same as the date of the pottery found in each one of them. Tomb 1 was used during the Myc. IIIA: 2-IIIB periods, and the types of vases from these deposits are jars, stirrup jars and shallow cups, that is, pottery suitable for burial goods and burial rites. A cooking pot, the only pottery item from tomb 3, has been dated in the Myc. IIIA: 1 period. Tomb 4 was used during the Myc. IIA, from which period there are an alabastron and a cup used for burial goods and rites respectively, and again was reused from the Myc. IIIA: 2/IIIB - Myc. IIIB/C periods. The pottery from these levels consists of closed forms for grave goods, with the exception of a domestic type tray, a vessel associated with ritual. Tomb 7 was in use from Myc. IIIA: 1 - Myc. IIIB. Stirrup jug, stirrup jar and alabastron are the dominant forms plus one pithos and Myc. IIIA: 1 kylix; a spouted cup was also, reportedly, found. With the exception of the kylix, the rest are wares used for burial goods. Tomb 8 was very poor; only a Myc. IIIC: 1 amphoriskos was found inside. Tomb 9 was used from Myc. IIIB/C: 1 form, and alabastron, jar, amphoriskos, a type of askos, and an arybalos of the Myc. IIIC: 1. A Myc. IIIC: 1 cup and a jug are the shapes appropriate for burial rites. IIB period. Tomb 25 was in use continuously from the Myc. IIIA: 1 through the Myc. IIIC: 1 period; stirrup jars and a cup are the Myc. IIIA vases, while the Myc. Tomb 26 is the one of the two tombs at Kolonaki which was used during the Myc. I period; this makes it, along with Hagia Anna tomb 2 and Ismenion tomb 2, the oldest Mycenaean burials in Thebes. This is the only tomb with MH matt-painted wares. Vessels for burial rites, such as kylix and cups, belong to the Myc. I deposit and a bridge spouted jugs belong to the Myc. Very few vases, among those which could not be located, were described as being painted. 60 MYCENAEAN POTTERY AND FIGURINES KERAMOPOULLOS EXCAVATIONS The computation of the motifs shows commonality in themes, and also absence of pictorial subjects such as man, chariots, animals, themes inspired by the sea such as fish, linked whorl-shell, seaweed, sponge print, and ship with the exception of the cuttlefish and the argonaut. Absent as well are diagonal and arcade patterns and the batched loop. The pottery rarely displays religious symbolism both in shapes and decoration, thus the themes of horns of consecration and adder mark are not present; the double axe appears once on a Myc. I alabastron. The correlation of the cemeteries with the palace dates shows that sixteen tombs date in the proto-palatial period, that is, within Myc. IIIA:1 and earlier. Ten tombs continue to be used during the Myc. IIIB phase, when most buildings in Thebes were constructed. Six tombs continue to be used also during the Myc. IIIC, three tombs were used only during the Myc. IIIC, and three were reused during the Myc. IIIC after a break during the Myc. IIIB. The frequency and dates of use and reuse of the tombs are in agreement with the history of the Kadmeia. An X-Ray Detraction analysis of some of the specimens would enable scholars to identify the local and foreign clays, data which would verify the local and /or pottery imported in Thebes. The closest similarities of the pottery are those from Elateia, Iolkos and Prosymna. As for a local “school” there is no evidence of distinctive styles to diffenciate the pottery from the Furumark clarification, such as suggested by Julie Hruby for Pylos 262 . Nevertheless, occasional isolated items show a “free spirit” of a local artist in the pottery and the figurines. Certain observations concerning the Mycenaean cemeteries of Thebes should be made here 263 . Keramopoullos and other scholars following him have ascribed the larger chamber tombs to earlier Mycenaean dates and the smaller tombs to later dates. This assertion should be reconsidered after the recent excavations at Kastellia, where the Myc. IIIB tombs are some of the largest known, 80 m 2 , and they are later than some of the Myc. I tombs at the Kolonaki - Hagia Anna cemeteries, which average ca. 15 m 2. The Mycenaean cemeteries in Thebes consist of chamber tombs only, over 120 of which have been identified and/or investigated. Their shapes are polymorphous, and they do not have any characteristics that should be seen as local. Characteristic, though, of the Theban tombs is the relative frequency of plastered and painted walls. The better-known ones are the frescos from the Megalo Kastelli tomb excavated in the 1970s 264 . In addition to the above, traces of frescos were found at a tomb at the 1960s excavations at Kolonaki and also at Kolonaki, t. 15, where the 262. The holes and grooves for hinges at the front of niches inside a chambered tomb at Megalo Kastelli, excavated in the 1960s, proved Keramopoullos to be right. Inhumation and cremation were both practiced in Thebes, inhuma-tion being used more frequently. Enough information has been provided to allow the following remarks: Tombs contained single and multiple burials; inhumation could take place in the dromos of a tomb, such as in the case of t. 2 at Hagia Anna dated in Myc. IIIB, and in the dromos of t. 10 at Kolonaki dated in Myc. IIIC. The bodies were placed either lengthwise or on their backs with knees bent; the latter position was not necessitated by the smallness of the tomb which suggests an imitation of the “seated” position. The date of the burials with bent knees ranges from Myc. II through Myc. IIIB. Burials of children appear exclusively at Kolonaki tombs 1 and 2, but this separation by age is not the rule. Children were buried along with adults and in similar positions with them. Cremation has been reported from tombs 4, possibly 9, 14, 16, 26 at Kolonaki, and t. 2 at Hagia Anna, as well as from a Kastelli tomb excavated in the 1970s. The cremations had one or more of the following characteristics: Burned human bones were found on the floor of the tomb but no ashes (Kolonaki t. 16); ashes from cremation inside three-handled jars (Kolonaki t. 26), or pithoid jar (Kastelli), or alabastra. The cremation took place outside the chamber; spread charcoal (Kolonaki t. 9) and a pile of ashes near an inhumation (Hagia Anna t. 2) were results of activities requiring less intense fire than a cremation would. The cremation in Kolonaki t. 14 could be dated anywhere from Myc. I to Myc. IIIC; more precise is the cremation in Kolonaki t. 16, which is dated in Myc. IIIB. The earliest cremations are noted in Kolonaki t. 26 and Hagia Anna t. 2, which date in Myc. II. A wooden plastered sarcophagos which belonged to a child’s burial was found in t. 24 at Kolonaki 265 . Wooden sarcophagoi are rarely found, with single examples from the Athenian Agora, Dendra, Prosymna, and Crete. Animal bones from dogs and boar came from inside three tombs at Kolonaki resulting, possibly, from sacrifices or funerary meals. The presence of pottery such as kylikes and domestic-type vessels, along with steatite buttons and a few other pieces of jewelry at the dromos, support the “clean up” theory before a new burial; a good example of the practice is the case of t. 25 at Kolonaki, where shards of the same vase were collected from the dromos and from inside the tomb. Funerary feasts are attested by the cooking pots found in the dromos and also inside the tombs, some of which were associated with charcoal remains. The frescoed tombs, the wooden sarcophagoi, the practice of crema-tion, while they are not unique, are noticeable for their frequency in Thebes. For similarities of those practices, one looks more toward Euboea and further into the Argolid and Crete, which picture is suggestive of sea routes of contact. Contacts with Attica are more evident in Boeotian regions east of Thebes. 62 MYCENAEAN POTTERY AND FIGURINES KERAMOPOULLOS EXCAVATIONS TABLE I Periods of Use of Each Tomb – Kolonaki Cemetery TABLES 63

MYCENAEAN PICTORIAL POTTERY 

# FROM THE ARGIVE HERAION  

> (PLATES

112-116) 

EXCAVATIONS conducted over the years at the site of the sanctuary of Hera near 

Argos (also called Prosymna) have revealed extensive evidence for Mycenaean occu-

pation.1 Considerable quantities of pottery, dating no later than LH IIIB:2, were discov-

ered in both settlement areas and tombs.2 After a gap, the site appears to have been reused, 

as a cult center, from the Geometric period onwards.3 

Among the finds made in the Mycenaean settlement areas during American excavations 

under the direction of Charles Waldstein (later Sir Charles Walston) in 1892-1895 are 

fragments from at least nine vases with pictorial decoration. These have no recorded find-

spots and are at present kept in the storerooms of the National Museum at Athens. Al-

though all but one have been illustrated in print, the fragments deserve further study.

in outline, of second figure, his solid feet or footgear 

placed at lower level than those of man to right, just 

above separate "base line"; higher up, at level of

to left. On the other side, solid feet of another male

Too little survives to reconstruct the original design on this LH IIIB deep bowl 

(FS 284).4 It is surely unwarranted to interpret the intriguing remains, even tentatively, as 

"an unskilled version of a traditional dance before a sacred tree."5 On the first side, the man 

to the right is standing before, or moving slowly towards, what must be a poorly drawn tree, 

while raising his arm, perhaps in salute. The other man on this side is in a similar, quiet 

stance but is heading away from the tree, judging from the direction of his feet. At the same 

time, the possibility cannot be excluded that he is looking back, depending on the interpreta-

tion of what may be his raised arm. 

There is no parallel for such a composition, nor indeed for the extremely crude style of 

execution. Long-legged men, seemingly naked and with muscular calves, are well known in 

Mycenaean pictorial vase painting, where they are seen engaged in a variety of activities.6 

Nevertheless, none is shown with such grossly exaggerated thighs and sticklike torso as the 

best preserved of the figures on 1. 

It is even more difficult to reconstruct the original scene on the other side of the vase, 

which included another male figure above a "base line". The two oblique lines behind the 

man are not readily explained. They do not suggest branches of a tree such as are seen on 

the other side, since they are placed at a relatively much lower level and face downwards. 

One of them could be the tail end of the painted band at the base of the handle.

several better-preserved pottery representations of bovids (but not of other animals) with

The original krater, of the neckless (FS 7-9) or deep-bowl (FS 281) type, must date to 

LH IIIB, like other Mycenaean vases with bull-protome designs.9 They derive from sites in 

the Argolid as well as Cyprus and include at least one krater of deep-bowl type similarly 

decorated with a frieze of protomes facing right.10 

By comparison with the other vase representations, the protomes on 3 are very clumsily 

drawn: they lack well-defined heads and have muzzles reduced to a series of sharp curves. 

On the other hand, the thick outline, wavy on the inside, is a feature of some other bull

The bird may have been shown with its head turned back, assuming the trace of paint at 

the lower right edge belongs to its neck or body. Birds in this pose are well known in Myce-

naean vase painting. 15 Alternatively, the trace of paint may belong to a column of horizontal 

dashes, a well-known Mycenaean subsidiary motif. An interesting detail is the row of curv-

ing strokes on the beak. They are probably purely decorative and recall the fringe hanging 

from the beak of the bird on a krater fragment from Tiryns of similar, LH IIIB date."6

The original large bowl with a crowded scene of fish and subsidiary motifs on its inte-

rior must have been an attractive vase, the fish swimming in liquid when the bowl was

ments from Mycenae). MYCENAEAN PICTORIAL POTTERY FROM THE ARGIVE HERAION 497 

filled. There are no close parallels for this particular combination of shape and decoration 

among the numerous fish representations in Mycenaean vase painting. Most Mycenaean 

representations simply show fish swimming horizontally to the right, but there are also 

several with an emphasis on upward or downward movement and the concomitant use of an 

extended zone of decoration.19 The Mycenaean repertoire includes some shallow bowls 

with fish on the interior and less elaborate, mainly linear decoration outside,20 but these 

bowls are usually much smaller than 8 and have not such a prominent, upward-sloping rim 

with patterns painted on top. 

In fact, 8 may be more at home in Crete: with its particular shape and style of deco-

ration, a fragment of a ring-based, shallow bowl of LM II-111A:1 from the Northwest 

House at Knossos springs to mind.2" This bowl has a patterned rim and an elegant composi-

tion of fish swimming in different directions in an explicitly marine setting on the interior; 

it also has a zone of flowers between a rim band and line group on the outside. Its fish are 

rendered differently from those on 8, which find a rather better parallel on a LM II bridge-

spouted jug from Katsamba near Knossos.22 This vessel carries a highly elaborate, "free-

field" composition of fish and birds placed at varying angles. 

At the same time, it should be noted that the leaf pattern depicted on the outside of 8

cannot be readily paralleled, whether in Crete or in mainland Greece. The fringed band 

below the rim on the interior, on the other hand, does recall a fragmentary krater from 

Tiryns, which is surely Mycenaean and dates to LH IIIA: 1 or early IIIA:2.23 On this krater 

a series of oblique strokes is seen rising from a band below the handle zone which includes 

one large fish and several examples of the single wavy-line motif that is also shown between 

the two best-preserved fish on 8. This subsidiary motif, which recurs as groups of parallel 

wavy lines on other early Mycenaean fish-krater fragments,24 presumably derives from the 

trailing corals growing out of rockwork seen in Minoan representations.25 

The original bowl of 8 may then be either an import from Crete or an early Mycenaean 

pictorial piece with Minoan prototypes influencing both its shape and fish design.26

Too little remains of this coarse, closed vessel with its rather crudely drawn but lively 

fish representation to determine its shape and date. Indeed, it is difficult to classify the 

(incomplete) composition of differently-sized fish as well as the details of their rendering 

among Mycenaean representations of fish. The presence of what is probably some kind of 

marine vegetation at the upper right edge of the fragment seems to be an early (LH IIIA:1 

or IIIA:2 early) feature, deriving from Minoan prototypes (see 8). 

In addition to these fragments from the Mycenaean settlement at the Argive Heraion, 

there are three whole pots with pictorial decoration from Waldstein's and later excavations 

of chamber tombs of the period. One is a squat alabastron with fish (a), possibly dating as 

early as LH IIIA:1,27 another a LH IIIB jug with goats (b).28 The third is a spouted, one-

handled cup of LH IIIA:2-IIIB decorated with birds (c).29 Considering the large number of 

Mycenaean tombs excavated at the site (over fifty-five) with their numerous decorated 

vases, the amount of pictorial pottery from the tombs is exceedingly small. The same obser-

vation can be made with regard to Mycenaean tombs at other sites in the Argolid and 

elsewhere in mainland Greece. Most pictorial pottery derives from settlement (i.e., domestic 

or other non-funerary) contexts, but even then it usually represents only a tiny fraction of 

all Mycenaean decorated pottery found at the site in question. A notable exception is the 

so-called Potter's Quarter at Berbati in the Argolid, which yielded many fragments of 

LH IIIA:2-IIIB kraters with pictorial decoration similar to that found in Cyprus and the 

Levant, as well as several misfired pieces. This establishment may then have produced 

pictorial vases mainly for export to the east.30 

As for the dating of the pictorial material from the Argive Heraion discussed here, it is 

based on a comparison of vase shapes, motifs, and styles of decoration. Probably earliest is the 

Minoan or Mycenaean bowl fragment with fish (8), dating to LM II-IIIA: 1/LH IIIA: 1; the

tomb WI). 6 falls within the LH IIIA:2-IIIB range (as does c), while most others (1-5, 7; 

also b) may be more definitely attributed to LH IIIB and most probably to LH IIIB: 1. 

These pictorial finds represent a fairly wide range of vase shapes, chiefly open (1-8, 

also c) but rarely closed (9; but see a and b, from tombs). The open shapes are mainly 

kraters (2-6), but whether of the neckless type with vertical strap handles (FS 7-9; Mount-

joy 1986, figs. 70, 99, 134, 135, 156) or of the deep-bowl type with horizontal loop handles 

and a low ring base (FS 281; Mountjoy 1986, figs. 142, 159) is in most cases not clear. 4, 

with its trace of a handle attachment, is definitely of the deep-bowl type. It should be noted 

that the deep-bowl krater is the most commonly found shape for pictorial decoration in 

LH IIIB settlement contexts at other sites in the Argolid, such as Mycenae and Tiryns. 

Interestingly, the material here includes two examples of deep bowls (1, 7; FS 284; Mount-

joy 1986, figs. 143, 160, 161), a shape that was not often used for pictorial decoration in 

LH IIIB. 8 formed part of a large bowl which cannot be readily matched in the Mycenaean 

repertoire of vase shapes but seems rather to be Minoan. 

With regard to the pictorial designs, the fragments vary a good deal to include human 

figures (1), a bull (2) and bull protomes (3, 4), birds (5-7, also c), and fish (8, 9, also a). To 

these may be added the goats of b. 

There can be little doubt that most of this Mycenaean pictorial material was made in 

the Argolid, as it conforms to the standard LH IIIA-IIIB products from this part of Greece. 

One fish fragment (9), in contrast, is decidedly inferior in fabric, being made of coarse, gritty 

clay which may suggest a different origin. Another piece (8), from a large bowl with a lively 

composition of fish and subsidiary marine elements on its interior and leaf-shaped motifs on 

the outside, may possibly be an import from Crete. In any case, its fish design must hark 

back to Minoan marine representations of LM Il-111A:1. 

Apart from 8, some other fragments have interesting connections, too. 3 and 4, both 

showing bull protomes, may be attributed to the same painter, although not to the same 

LH IIIB krater. The bull-protome design is known from other mainland sites as well as 

from Cyprus, the latter occurrences probably representing imports. The parallels, however, 

are not close enough to suggest the painter recognized at the Argive Heraion. 

What remains of the birds on the deep-bowl fragments (7a-d) has good parallels else-

where in the Argolid, including Berbati. 

Other pictorial pieces are less easily matched. They include the deep bowl with its 

enigmatic scene of human figures and a tree (1), as well as two vases from tombs: the one-

handled bowl (c) with four clumsily drawn birds on the interior and the fish alabastron (a), 

the only pictorial vase definitely of this shape. 

To conclude, the Argive Heraion may be classed as an important find-place of Myce-

naean pictorial pottery of LH IIIA-IIIB in the Argolid, after Mycenae, Tiryns, and Ber-

bati,3' yielding both mainstream and unusual examples.
